docs.title: Urban Solar Carver
docs.text:
GPU-accelerated generation of maximum developable building volumes that protect solar and daylight access in urban environments.

USC works by subtraction: it starts from a theoretical maximum volume, casts rays from the protected surfaces toward the sky, and removes the voxels that obstruct solar or daylight access beyond a configurable threshold.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
• 6 carving modes covering solar access, passive heating, daylighting, and radiative cooling
  • 3-stage pipeline (preprocessing, thresholding, exporting); each stage can be re-run on its own
  • GPU-accelerated ray tracing via NVIDIA Warp (DDA kernel), with CPU fallback
  • Grasshopper plugin (27 components) for Rhino 3D integration
  • Python API, CLI, and Jupyter notebooks

docs.title: Pipeline
docs.text:
Input (PLY meshes, EPW weather, YAML config)
    |
    v
Preprocessing ── scores.npy, voxel_grid.npy
    |
    v
Thresholding ─── mask.npy (binary carving mask)
    |
    v
Exporting ────── export.ply (or .obj/.stl/.glb, set by final_mesh_format)

Each stage reads the previous stage's manifest, so you can re-run thresholding with different parameters without re-computing scores.

docs.title: Grasshopper Plugin (Rhino 3D)
docs.text: USC provides 27 custom Grasshopper components for visual parametric workflows in Rhino.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: Copy all .ghuser files from grasshopper/USC_GHplugin/ to your Grasshopper User Objects folder, or drag them onto the Grasshopper canvas. Requires Rhino 8 (the components are Python 3 script components).

docs.title: Updating components on existing canvases
docs.text:
Components already placed on a canvas keep the code they were placed with. After installing new .ghuser files, drop USC_SyncCanvas (ribbon: Session) on the canvas:

  1. Leave update unconnected and read report: it lists which USC components are up to date and which would change. Components whose code you edited by hand count as outdated and would be overwritten.
  2. Connect a Button to update and click it. Components whose inputs and outputs are unchanged are replaced in place, keeping position, wires, internalised values (Set One String), graft/flatten/simplify settings, enabled/preview state and group membership. Components whose inputs or outputs changed are placed beside the old one inside a red group that names the new or removed ports: rewire the new component, then delete the old one and the group.
  3. The whole update is one undo step (Ctrl+Z). If anything fails mid-update, the canvas is rolled back and the error appears in report.

By default the updates come from the installed user objects (Grasshopper's User Objects folders); wire a folder path into folder to update from elsewhere, e.g. grasshopper/USC_GHplugin in a checkout.

docs.title: Rebuilding the components
docs.text:
The .ghuser files are generated from the sources in grasshopper/components/; edit the .py, never the .ghuser. Each source declares its own ports: names and descriptions in its "GH UI" block, order and types in the numpydoc Inputs / Outputs docstring. grasshopper/components.json holds the ribbon subcategory and the stable user-object GUID; icons are grasshopper/icons/<source name>.png (24x24).

Code shared by several components (daemon calls, the run command wrapper run_stages, engine issues shown as warnings by show_issues, loading the engine's mode_registry.py and archetype_defaults.py by path with engine_module, PLY reading and writing, mesh conversion, override parsing) lives in grasshopper/usc_gh.py. The components load it at run time from <carver_root>/grasshopper/, where carver_root is the repository folder given to USC_Session, so editing it takes effect on the next solve without rebuilding any .ghuser. It uses only the standard library, RhinoCommon and the Grasshopper SDK, because the component scripts run in Rhino's own Python, not in the USC environment.

pip install -e .[ghbuild]                       # pythonnet
python grasshopper/build_ghuser.py              # rebuild into USC_GHplugin/
python grasshopper/build_ghuser.py --check      # exit 1 if any .ghuser is stale

The builder uses GH_IO.dll from the Rhino 8 install (--ghio <folder> to point elsewhere); Rhino does not need to be running. Rebuilds are byte-for-byte reproducible, so an unchanged source leaves its .ghuser untouched. tests/test_gh_components.py checks that every source's UI block matches its docstring and that every docstring type maps to a Grasshopper type hint.

A component already placed on a saved canvas keeps the code it was placed with; USC_SyncCanvas updates it (see above).

docs.title: Smoke test in Rhino
docs.text:
tools/grasshopper_example_smoke_test.py solves examples/USC_components_for_grasshopper.gh in a running Rhino 8 (through RhinoCode.exe) and compares two runs, for example main against a branch. It needs Rhino open, so it is not part of pytest. Run it with the USC environment's python:

python tools/grasshopper_example_smoke_test.py run main D:\path\to\urbanSolarCarver
python tools/grasshopper_example_smoke_test.py run branch D:\path\to\worktree
python tools/grasshopper_example_smoke_test.py compare main branch

run stops any running daemon, fills the template definition in memory (root panel, output folders, EPW, start_daemon and run toggles, pipeline 1's geometry from examples/test_inputs/multiple_buildings), solves it with the root's usc_gh.py and daemon, stops the daemon again and closes the definition without saving. A root without .venv, venv or python_path.txt (a worktree) gets a python_path.txt pointing at the python running the script. The report (messages and output counts of every USC component) and the output folders go to ~/.urbansolarcarver/gh_runs/<label>, a short path because deep output folders exceed Windows' 260-character limit. Each run keeps its output there (about 120 MB for the example), replaced by the next run with the same label; delete the folder when done. The definition's start_daemon toggle also switches on verbose, so the daemon opens its own console window during a run. With several Rhinos open, pass --rhino <ID> from RhinoCode.exe list.

compare matches components by nickname and occurrence, compares their messages (paths, ids and timings removed) and output counts, the meshes byte for byte, integer and boolean arrays (masks) exactly and float arrays (scores) to a relative difference of 1e-5, since GPU atomic adds sum in a varying order (about 1e-7 between runs). It exits with 1 when anything differs.

docs.title: Daemon
docs.text:
The components send their work to a persistent daemon process that keeps the CUDA context and compiled kernels loaded, so repeated runs skip the start-up cost:

urbansolarcarver daemon start       # start GPU daemon
# ... use Grasshopper components ...
urbansolarcarver daemon stop        # stop when done

The daemon binds to localhost only. Clients authenticate with a random key that the daemon generates on first start and stores in ~/.urbansolarcarver/.daemon_authkey.

docs.title: Components
docs.text:
The ribbon shows each component as USC <Name> (for example USC Session). Below they are listed by their source file name in grasshopper/components/, grouped by ribbon tab.

Session (0::Session)

  • USC_Session: finds the USC Python environment and starts or checks the daemon. Wire a Boolean True to start_daemon to launch the daemon; when the input is unconnected or False, the component only reports whether a daemon is running.
  • USC_SyncCanvas: updates the USC components on the canvas to the installed versions (see Updating components on existing canvases)

Configuration (1::Config)

  • USC_Config: builds a pipeline configuration from a mode, an EPW path, an output folder, an optional base YAML and the override strings of the parameter components below. With no YAML, the daemon starts from the mode's starting values (for example the analysis period of the benefit, irradiance and time-based modes) and applies the overrides; configs/ is not read. Spellings such as time_based or tilted-plane are accepted.
  • USC_Mode: selects the carving mode by number and outputs its name for USC_Config's mode input. The mode list and descriptions come from the engine (mode_registry.py), so solve USC_Session first; without it the component shows a message that says so.
  • USC_EPW (USC EPW Path): passes the EPW file path
  • USC_AnalysisPeriod: defines the analysis date/time range
  • USC_GridSettings: voxel size, surface sampling spacing (grid_step), grid padding (margin_frac)
  • USC_RaySettings: ray length, minimum sun altitude, north direction (north_deg)
  • USC_BenefitParams: benefit-mode hour weighting: balance temperature and offset (simple weights), or a simulated_weights.json artifact plus the experimental include_harm toggle (simulated weights)
  • USC_TiltedPlane: fixed-angle envelope parameters
  • USC_RadCooling (USC Radiative Cooling): radiative cooling parameters (dew point, Bliss constant)
  • USC_Threshold: thresholding strategy, score smoothing, column carve-above post-processing, and the slope limit (max_slope; empty = 75 degrees for the weighted modes, 90 = off). Connect its output to USC_ThresholdStage's threshold_overrides input (not Config) so threshold changes only re-run thresholding.
  • USC_Postprocess: smoothing and cleanup settings. Connect its output to USC_Export's postprocess_overrides input (not Config) so mesh cleanup changes only re-run export.
  • USC_Diagnostics: detailed score statistics and diagnostic plot images

Pipeline execution (2::Main)

  • USC_RunPipeline: runs all three stages in one go (quick prototyping)

  • USC_Preprocess: runs preprocessing only (ray tracing + scoring). Errors turn the component red.

  • USC_ThresholdStage: runs thresholding only. Accepts threshold_overrides directly. Its summary shows the slope limit (angle, voxels removed, share of the obstruction score). Errors turn the component red.

  • USC_Export: runs exporting only. Accepts postprocess_overrides directly. Errors turn the component red.
  • USC_Massing: stage 4, builds floor plates from the carving mask (inputs config, thr_result, massing_overrides, run; outputs closed Breps, floor areas per floor and in total, and the plates.json path). See Floor-plate massing.
  • USC_MassingSettings: floor heights, module size, tolerance and stacking for USC_Massing. Connect its output to USC_Massing's massing_overrides input so changes re-run only massing.

The stage components send the daemon's run command, each producing its own stage, and read the stage folders from the reply. A stage reads the output of the stage before it from <out_dir>/<stage> of its Config, so Preprocess and the stages after it need the same Config out_dir; the pre_result and thr_result inputs order the solve and still have to be connected. Conditions the engine reports (a setting the mode ignores, nothing carved, a footprint that could not be read, ...) appear as warnings on the component, one per issue, as <stage>: <message>. Re-running preprocessing makes the stages after it refuse their old output until they run again (the error names the stage to re-run).

Simulated weights (3::Weights)

  • USC_Archetype: assembles a typical building for the simulated weights from the five parameter families below; every input is optional (neutral defaults, read from the engine's archetype_defaults.py, so solve USC_Session first)
  • USC_ZoneGeometry / USC_ZoneFabric / USC_ZoneVent / USC_ZoneOperation / USC_ZoneShading: Honeybee-style family feeders for USC_Archetype: shoebox dimensions + per-facade window-to-wall ratio, envelope U-values + g-value + mass class, air-change rates + heat recovery, setpoints + internal gains, and declared shading coefficients. Each family is one wire into USC_Archetype.
  • USC_SimulateWeights: runs the ISO 13790 5R1C simulation through the daemon; outputs the simulated_weights.json path (wire into USC_BenefitParams) and a heatmap preview image

docs.title: Input geometry
docs.text: Test surfaces must be individual flat panels. If you are using extruded block boundaries or any joined polysurface, explode it into its faces before connecting it to USC_Preprocess. Otherwise the planarity check rejects the combined surface and preprocessing fails with a "No points sampled" error.

docs.title: Recommended workflow
docs.text:
Use the decomposed pipeline (Preprocess → ThresholdStage → Export as separate components) rather than RunPipeline. This lets you:

  • Adjust threshold parameters (USC_Threshold → USC_ThresholdStage) and re-export without re-running the expensive ray-tracing step.
  • Adjust mesh cleanup settings (USC_PostProcess → USC_Export) and regenerate the mesh without re-thresholding or re-preprocessing.

Only USC_Preprocess needs to re-run when you change geometry, mode, or the analysis period.

docs.title: Floor-plate massing
docs.text: The massing stage turns the carved envelope into stacked floor plates: a ground floor, then floors of equal height, each a closed prism whose outline follows the maximum volume's footprint and steps back where the envelope does not allow the floor. Use it for massing models, floor-area figures and as simulation input (one closed prism per floor and plate).

docs.title: How plates are formed
docs.text:
1. Footprint and facades. The footprint is the maximum volume's plan projection (the area it covers seen from above), so an uneven or raised base does not change it. Preprocessing saves this footprint (footprint.json in its folder, world coordinates) from the mesh it voxelized; massing reads that file, not the mesh in the config passed to massing and not the mesh file on disk, so later edits to either change nothing. If preprocessing could not compute a footprint, massing uses the outline of the occupied voxel columns and warns. The footprint outline is split into facades wherever it turns by more than 30 degrees. Curved or faceted outlines with smaller turns stay one facade. A facade whose vertices all lie within 1 cm of the line from its first to its last vertex is straight: footprints cut from meshes carry vertices micrometres off a straight wall. Far from the origin, where a mesh stored in float32 rounds its coordinates by more, the tolerance is four of those float32 steps, and it is never more than half a voxel. A real bend, a few degrees over a few metres, stays a bend.
  2. Faces. Every footprint column belongs to its nearest facade. Facades shorter than two modules (2 * min_plate_dimension: chamfers, small steps) get no face of their own; their neighbours meet at one corner across them. At corners the longer facade takes the corner square (up to half the building's depth behind it), so every face ends in a line perpendicular to its facade. At equal lengths (a square) the facade closer to the x axis takes the corner. Along a facade not aligned with the voxel grid, the voxelizer also fills columns whose centre lies just outside the footprint; such a column belongs to the face of the footprint point nearest to it, so the end of a slab is cut on the same lines as the rest of it.
  3. Bays. Each face is cut into square modules of min_plate_dimension (3 m): along its facade, perpendicular to it, and in depth behind it, parallel to it. Along a straight facade the rows of modules are laid from both ends of the building (its extent along the facade) towards the middle; what is left over widens the middle row, or the two middle rows equally (a 10 m bar: 3, 4 and 3 m; 13 m: 3, 3.5, 3.5 and 3 m). An end wing therefore starts with a whole row whatever the building's length, and the cuts on the two sides of a straight building line up. Along a curved facade the rows are cut every module of length from its start. A row narrower than a module at the end of a face that ends inside the building (at a corner square) joins its neighbour, and a module at the back of a row (where the face meets the one opposite) shallower than min_plate_dimension joins the one in front of it. Each module is built on its own, so a wing keeps its floors whatever the envelope does behind it in the same face, for example a courtyard of a perimeter block carved lower. Behind any facade a plate can therefore be as shallow as one module, min_plate_dimension.
  4. Floors. For each floor (ground floor ground_floor_height, then floor_height), a module is built when it stays inside the maximum volume over the floor's full height, at most plate_tolerance of its volume lies outside the carved envelope, and (with plate_stacking: supported) it is built on the floor below. A column along a facade not aligned with the voxel grid counts only for its share inside the footprint, so whether a module is built does not depend on the angle of the footprint to the grid. A module over the tolerance is not built even when built modules enclose it, so a local dip in the envelope can leave a hole of one or two modules in a floor; holes are not filled. Parts narrower than min_plate_dimension are dropped (the test is the same at any angle of the footprint to the voxel grid), so a strip one module deep, min_plate_dimension, is kept. The ground floor starts at the maximum volume's lowest point, and the top floor ends at or below its highest point; preprocessing records both in its manifest. The voxel grid is not aligned with these points, so the lowest occupied voxel layer can lie mostly below the base (its centre below it) and the highest mostly above the roof. Such a layer is filled only where rays hit the base or the roof, which they miss in columns along facades that are not aligned with the grid, so it does not count: a floor's height and its share outside the envelope are measured over the layers whose centre lies between the lowest and the highest point. A preprocessing run from before the manifest recorded these points starts the ground floor at the bottom of the lowest occupied layer and lets the top floor reach the top of the highest occupied layer, up to one voxel outside the maximum volume at each end; running preprocessing again gives the floors above.
  5. Plates. The connected built modules of a floor form a plate. A module on a straight facade is drawn as a rectangle in its facade's frame: cuts lie on the cut lines (along the facade and in depth), the back of the last module lies on the midline where the facade faces a parallel one, and the facade edges are the footprint's own. Other edges (face ends at corners) are within half a voxel of the voxel columns. Where a corner is not square, the faces of its two facades meet along the bisector of the corner; a module there is its rectangle cut by that line (or by a line of the two facades' corner squares, or by a bisector with a facade that meets one of them; where the faces meet along a curve, by the line midway between the two faces' columns turned to a direction of the two facades or their bisector), so it ends on one straight slanted edge. A cut that would leave an angle under 30 degrees or a piece narrower than a voxel is not used. Modules on curved facades, and the modules no such line separates from a neighbouring face, follow their voxel columns, straight to within half a voxel; they stay off the columns of modules not in the plate. Where the shapes of two modules overlap, the overlap belongs to one of them, so plates of different modules never overlap. Spikes and cracks of no width that the boolean operations leave are removed.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Setting Default Meaning ground_floor_height 5.0 Height of the ground floor (m) floor_height 3.0 Height of every floor above it (m) min_plate_dimension 3.0 Side of the square module and minimum plate width (m); "Grid module" in the browser UI plate_tolerance 0.2 Largest share of a module's volume on a floor outside the carved envelope; "Permitted volume exceedance" in the browser UI plate_stacking supported supported: build a module only on a built module; free: each floor on its own

Plates never leave the maximum volume. The three sizes must be at least the voxel size of the preprocessing run; the stage reports an error naming the setting otherwise.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
In <out_dir>/massing/:

  • plates.json: one entry per plate (floor, z bottom and top, outline and holes in world coordinates, area, number of modules (bays), share of its volume outside the envelope), plus the floor area per floor and in total;
  • plates.obj: one closed mesh per plate, named floor_<n>_plate_<m>, written whatever final_mesh_format says (the browser interface draws it and reads its parts by name);
  • plates.ply, plates.stl or plates.glb when final_mesh_format is one of them: the same plates, as one mesh in PLY and STL (formats without named parts) and with one named part per plate in GLB. The manifest names this file as export_mesh_path (plates.obj itself for OBJ). A change of final_mesh_format reruns massing as well as exporting. Far from the origin (georeferenced models) PLY keeps the coordinates in double precision and GLB places the offset in each node, while STL can only hold float32 and the run reports a float32_coordinates issue when that rounds them by more than 1 mm;
  • manifest.json and diagnostics/diagnostic.json (floors built, plates, floor areas, share of the carved envelope inside plates, volume placed outside the envelope through the tolerance, footprint source).

The run report gets a Massing section.

docs.title: Running it
docs.text:
• Python: massing(thr_result, cfg, out_dir)
  • CLI: usc massing -c config.yaml (finds the thresholding manifest of the run, or pass -f)
  • Grasshopper: USC_Massing after USC_ThresholdStage, with USC_MassingSettings

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Floors count from the lowest point of the maximum volume; a part that starts higher gets a warning (sloped ground is not supported yet).
  • If the maximum volume's footprint cannot be read from the mesh, or does not match the voxel grid (more than 5% of the occupied voxel columns more than one voxel outside it, for example when the file was replaced after preprocessing), the voxel footprint is used, with a warning; plates can then be up to one voxel larger than the true footprint.
  • Modules are rectangles in their face's frame; there are no interior zones (core, perimeter) and roofs are flat.

docs.title: Carving Modes
docs.text: USC supports six carving modes, each using a different strategy to determine which voxels to remove from the maximum buildable volume.

docs.title: Mode overview
docs.text: Mode Type Weight Source Requirements time-based Violation count Sun vectors from EPW EPW + analysis period irradiance Weighted Perez all-weather sky EPW + analysis period benefit Weighted Heating-benefit sky EPW + analysis period (+ balance temperature or a simulated-weights file) daylight Weighted CIE overcast luminance None (no EPW, no analysis period) tilted_plane Binary Geometric fixed angle Angle specification only radiative_cooling Weighted Martin-Berdahl + Bliss Dew point temperature (no EPW)

docs.title: Thresholding strategies
docs.text: USC supports three threshold strategies. The right choice depends on the mode.

docs.title: For weighted modes (irradiance, benefit, daylight, radiative_cooling)
docs.text:
Scores are continuous weighted sums: the sky-patch weight of every ray a voxel blocks, times the area of protected surface that ray's sample point stands for (about grid_step² m², times its edge_taper weight when that is set). The score is then a physical quantity that does not change with the sample spacing:

Mode Score unit A voxel's score is irradiance kWh the solar energy (direct and diffuse) it keeps from the protected surfaces over the analysis period benefit kWh the same for the heating-useful solar energy only (the hours below the balance point, or the simulated weights) daylight m² the overcast sky it hides from the protected surfaces, weighted by CIE overcast brightness, in m² of fully hidden sky radiative_cooling m² the night sky's cooling potential it hides, in m² of fully hidden sky

The patch weights of irradiance and benefit are kWh/m² per patch (Ladybug's sky matrix), counted on a surface facing the patch: there is no reduction for the angle at which a ray meets its surface, so the kWh are those a surface turned towards each sky patch would receive. The daylight and radiative_cooling weights are each patch's share of its sky and sum to 1, so 1 m² is the whole sky of 1 m² of open horizontal surface (a vertical facade sees half of it at most). Summed over a set of voxels a score counts what they block more than once when a ray crosses several of them; it compares voxels, it is not an energy balance. Scores written before this unit was introduced (preprocessing manifests without score_unit) were sums of patch weights without the area, and changed four times when the sample spacing halved.

Strategy How it works When to use carve_fraction (default) Removes the highest-scoring voxels until the removed part holds the target fraction of the building's total obstruction weight, counting the voxels that carve_above removes with them. 0.7 = aggressive (tall, slim volumes). 0.3 = conservative (bulky volumes). Recommended. Works as a slider; no knowledge of the score distribution needed. headtail Jiang (2013) head/tail breaks: splits the scores at their mean, then splits the part above the mean again, for as long as that part holds at most 40% of the values. Suited to heavy-tailed distributions. When you want an automatic, data-driven split without choosing a fraction. Numeric value Manual cutoff on the scores, in the score unit above. Voxels scoring above this value are carved. Advanced. Pick it from the score histogram in diagnostics/ (or the browser UI's). It means the same at any sample spacing, but depends on the weather, the period and the protected surfaces, so it carries over between variants of one project rather than between projects.

How carve_fraction and carve_above work together. With carve_above (the default), a column loses everything above its lowest removed voxel. Each voxel therefore goes at the cutoff of the lowest high-scoring voxel below it, and carve_fraction counts the score of everything removed that way: 0.4 removes 40% of the obstruction score. (Before this was counted, carve_above removed extra score on top of the value set, so 0.4 removed 50-62% in the ReSBE test blocks.)

Slope limit (max_slope_deg, default 75 degrees for these modes). Scores in a column are low near the ground, peak partway up and fall again, and a column is cut at its lowest voxel above the cutoff. Two neighbouring columns whose peaks fall just above and just below the cutoff end 10-15 m apart, and small score differences leave single-column spires. After carve_above, each column may rise at most tan(max_slope_deg) above a 5 x 5 median of its neighbours' heights; anything higher is removed. Cliffs become ramps and spires end one step above their surroundings. The limit only removes voxels, and carving more before it never keeps more after it. In the ReSBE test blocks (33 m, 0.5 m voxels) it cut the spike area from 26-186 m² to 0-25 m² for 0-10% of extra obstruction score, reported as obstruction_fraction_carved_by_slope_limit (it is not counted in carve_fraction). The median window and the allowed step are counted in voxels, so at 1 m voxels the limit is weaker than at 0.5 m. 90 turns it off. Finer sampling (grid_step) reduces spikes only a little; they come from the column rule, not from rays missing voxels.

All three strategies, the score smoothing and the reported retention consider occupied voxels only. Rays also cross the empty cells of streets, courtyards and the grid margin, and those cells typically hold 60-80% of the total score mass; including them would make the result depend on how much air the grid contains.

docs.title: For violation-count modes (time-based, tilted_plane)
docs.text:
time-based scores measure how much protected surface a voxel shades, and for how long, in m²·h: the shaded test-surface area times the duration, summed over the analysis period. Each sample point stands for about grid_step² m² of surface and each sun position for 1/sun_steps_per_hour h, so the score does not depend on the sampling density.

Threshold value Meaning 0 (default) Strict: remove any voxel that shades any protected surface at any sampled moment 5 Tolerate a voxel that shades up to 5 m²·h, e.g. 5 m² of facade for one hour, or 1 m² for five hours None Uses the default (0 = strict)

String strategies (carve_fraction, headtail) do not apply to violation counts and raise an error. tilted_plane is strictly binary (see below).

Physically interpretable thresholds

The time-based threshold has a direct meaning: threshold: 0 means zero shadow tolerance during the analysis period; threshold: 5 lets each voxel cast up to 5 m²·h of shadow on the protected surfaces. A numeric threshold of a weighted mode is read the same way in its unit: threshold: 20 in irradiance keeps a voxel that blocks up to 20 kWh over the period.

docs.title: time-based
docs.text:
Casts rays from test surfaces along actual sun vectors for specific dates and times. Each voxel's score is the shading it causes (m²·h, see above); with the default threshold: 0, a voxel is carved if any sun ray passes through it. There is no sky-patch weighting.

The sun is sampled sun_steps_per_hour times per hour (default 12, i.e. every 5 minutes). The sun moves about 15° of azimuth per hour, so hourly sampling leaves gaps between the ray sheets of consecutive hours in which mass survives while still shading the protected surface between samples; at 1 m voxels, 5-minute sampling closes them for obstructions up to ~40 m away. Ray count grows linearly with this value.

docs.title: Time basis: standard, daylight saving or solar time (time_basis)
docs.text:
By default (time_basis: standard) the hours of the analysis period are the EPW's local standard time.

With time_basis: daylight_saving they are daylight saving (summer) time: standard time plus one hour, on every date of the period, so 13:00 is read as 12:00 standard time. Weather files carry no daylight saving dates (TMY files leave the EPW header's field empty), so USC does not look up when the clocks change: a period that runs past the change of the clocks is one hour off on the days outside summer time. Split such a period, or use standard time.

With time_basis: solar they are true solar time: 12:00 is the moment the sun crosses the meridian, due south at a northern mid-latitude site, on every date. Solar-fence rules (Boulder: 21 December, two hours each side of solar noon) and the Japanese shadow regulation define their hours this way.

The two clocks differ by the equation of time (between about −14 and +16 minutes over the year) plus the site's distance from its time-zone meridian (4 minutes per degree of longitude). Solar noon in standard time:

Site 11 Feb 21 Jun 3 Nov 21 Dec Golden, CO (bundled EPW, 105.2° W, UTC−7) 12:15 12:03 11:44 11:59 Athens (23.7° E, UTC+2) 12:39 12:27 12:09 12:23

So a 10:00-14:00 window read in standard time is up to 39 minutes off a 10:00-14:00 solar-time rule in Athens, and the carved envelope shifts with it. Ladybug computes the sun position in either clock (is_solar_time).

time_basis is read by time-based only. daylight_saving and solar are refused in irradiance and benefit: their analysis period selects hourly EPW records, which are in standard time, so reading the period in another clock would pair each hour with the wrong weather record. Modes without an analysis period (daylight, tilted_plane, radiative_cooling) ignore it with the usual "does not use" warning. In the browser UI it is Time (Standard time / Daylight saving time / Solar time) under "More sun settings"; in Grasshopper it is the time_basis text input of USC Analysis Period.

mode: time-based
analysis_period: {st_month: 12, st_day: 21, st_hour: 10, end_month: 12, end_day: 21, end_hour: 14}
time_basis: solar   # 10:00-14:00 true solar time

Use case: protect direct sunlight during specific hours (e.g., winter solstice 10:00-14:00).

Threshold semantics: see violation-count thresholds above.

docs.title: irradiance
docs.text:
Weights each Tregenza sky patch by its cumulative direct + diffuse irradiance over the analysis period, using the Perez all-weather sky model. Voxels blocking high-irradiance patches receive higher scores.

Use case: climate-based solar resource assessment over an entire heating or cooling season.

docs.title: benefit
docs.text:
Similar to irradiance, but weights hours by a heating-benefit criterion. Two weightings are available:

Simple weights (default): only hours when the outdoor temperature is below balance_temperature - balance_offset contribute to patch weights. This protects solar access in the hours when it is useful for passive heating.

Use case: maximize passive solar heating potential during the heating season.

Key parameters: balance_temperature (free-running balance point; default 15 °C, typically about 12 °C for commercial to 18 °C for residential buildings), balance_offset (dead-band width, default 2 °C).

Cold period: urbansolarcarver.cold_period.cold_period_from_weather_file(epw_path, base_temperature) gives the start and end dates of the site's cold period, to use as the analysis period: the longest run of days whose 31-day running mean dry-bulb temperature (wrapping across the new year) is below the base, for benefit mode balance_temperature - balance_offset. It may wrap across the new year. Hours the EPW marks missing (99.9) are left out. The browser UI offers it as a preset of the analysis period. With simulated_weights_path set, the balance values are unused by the mode, so the cold period found from them describes the simple rule, not the simulated building. In climates whose temperature stays near the base all year, the longest run can be short and its dates arbitrary.

docs.title: Simulated weights
docs.text:
Instead of the binary cold-hour rule, benefit mode can consume hourly weights derived from a thermal simulation of a typical building (the compact 5R1C hourly model from ISO 13790). For every hour of the year the simulation answers: if one extra watt of sun arrived in this hour, how much less heating, and how much more cooling, would the building need over the whole year? This captures thermal lag (a noon gain stored in the mass and released into the cold evening still earns credit), diurnal mass state, and gain saturation, none of which the binary rule can express. The simple rule is the special case where the weights are 0 or 1.

Generate the weights once from an EPW and a building archetype (roughly ten numbers describing a typical building; the easiest form is a shoebox with per-facade window-to-wall ratios, see configs/archetype_example.yaml):

urbansolarcarver simulate-weights -e weather.epw -a configs/archetype_example.yaml

This writes simulated_weights.json (the weights plus full provenance) and a .png preview of the weights next to it. Then point a benefit config at the artifact:

mode: benefit
simulated_weights_path: simulated_weights.json
# include_harm: true   # experimental: also subtract summer-overheating contributions

A full-year analysis_period is the natural choice with simulated weights, since the schedule itself selects the useful hours. balance_temperature / balance_offset are unused (USC warns if you customize them). With diagnostic_plots: true, the run's diagnostics include a comparison dome showing how the simulated weights shifted the sky relative to the simple rule.

Use case: benefit envelopes that respond to the thermal mass, insulation, and glazing of the building stock being protected.

Key parameters: simulated_weights_path, include_harm (experimental; without declared seasonal shading (shading_hot in the archetype) harm is overstated, so treat it as a bracketing scenario).

See Simulated Benefit Weights for the engine's documentation (what it implements, how it was validated against RC_BuildingSimulator, the archetype inputs, and the declared limitations) and Tutorial 5 (examples/5_benefit_5r1c.ipynb) for an end-to-end walkthrough.

docs.title: daylight
docs.text:
Weights sky patches using the CIE standard overcast sky luminance distribution. Direct sun is not considered: each patch's weight is its overcast-sky luminance, which depends on the zenith angle, times its solid angle, scaled so the weights sum to 1. No weather file or analysis period is needed.

Use case: protect diffuse daylight access (e.g., for daylighting codes, visual comfort).

docs.title: tilted_plane
docs.text:
Traditional geometric solar envelope method. Every voxel above a tilted plane at a fixed angle from each test surface is carved. No weather data is involved. Each sample point casts one ray at the plane angle, outward along the facade's horizontal normal, and every voxel at or above that ray in its (x, y) column is removed: the whole half-space above the plane, not only the band the rays cross. Where two test-surface panels meet at a convex corner or kink, their rays diverge; extra rays from the corner sweep the headings between the two normals, so the plane rotates around the corner (at 45 degrees, a column outside a right-angle corner is capped at its distance from the corner). Concave corners need no extra rays: the two planes already meet there.

The angle can be a single float (applied uniformly) or a list of 8 floats (one per compass octant N, NE, E, SE, S, SW, W, NW, chosen by the direction each facade faces).

Use case: quick regulatory envelopes, traditional Knowles-style solar access planes.

Key parameter: tilted_plane_angle_deg

Threshold semantics: this mode is strictly binary: a voxel either protrudes above the cut plane or it does not. Do not set threshold; leave it unset (the default None). Setting any string method or a numeric value > 0 raises a validation error.

docs.title: radiative_cooling (experimental)
docs.text:
Weights sky patches by their radiative cooling potential, using the Martin-Berdahl atmospheric emissivity model and a Bliss angular attenuation factor. The aim is to keep access to the cold sky dome for passive nighttime cooling. The model uses one representative night-time dew point and reads no weather file.

Use case: hot-arid climates where nighttime radiative cooling is a significant design strategy.

Key parameters: dew_point_celsius, bliss_k, min_sky_elevation_deg (optional: ignore sky patches below this elevation and renormalize the rest)

Warning

This mode is experimental. The clear-sky assumption may not hold in humid or cloudy climates.

Horizontal surface assumption

The current implementation assumes a horizontal analysis surface (flat roof). The angular view-factor weighting (cosθ/π) is only valid for upward-facing surfaces. Applying these weights to tilted or vertical test surfaces will over-weight the zenith and under-weight low-altitude sky patches, producing inaccurate cooling envelopes.

docs.title: Pipeline orchestration
docs.text: File Purpose __init__.py Package entry point. load_config, build_config and user_config are imported directly; run_pipeline, PipelineResult, stages_to_rerun, the four stage functions and their result types are loaded from api.py on first access, so import urbansolarcarver and light CLI commands do not import torch or Warp. api.py Public facade. Defines run_pipeline(config, out_dir, produce, start_from, context), the sequencer: it runs the stages needed for produce, each writing into <out_dir>/<stage>, and returns a PipelineResult (one Result per stage that ran, plus the run's issues). Re-exports stages_to_rerun(), preprocessing(), thresholding(), exporting(), massing(), their result types, load_config() and build_config(). api_core/__init__.py Collects the three stage modules and their result types into one importable sub-package. api_core/preprocessing.py Stage 1. Voxelizes the max-volume mesh into a dense 3D grid, samples test surfaces into evenly spaced points with outward normals, generates rays toward sky patches (or sun positions, or the tilted-plane direction, depending on mode), traces them through the grid with the DDA kernel, and writes the per-voxel obstruction scores to scores.npy. Also writes voxel_grid.npy, footprint.json (the plan projection of the voxelized mesh, which massing reads), the sample points and normals, the manifest, and diagnostics (JSON always; plots with diagnostic_plots: true). api_core/thresholding.py Stage 2. Loads scores.npy from Stage 1, optionally applies Gaussian score smoothing (weighted modes), applies the selected thresholding strategy (carve_fraction, headtail, or a numeric cutoff) to the raw scores of the occupied voxels together with carve_above (column_postprocessing.carve_above_scores, so carve_fraction counts what carve_above removes), applies the slope limit (column_postprocessing.limit_column_slope; 75 degrees by default for the weighted modes), and writes the binary mask mask.npy and scores_compared_with_cutoff.npy (the values the cutoff was applied to, which the browser UI draws its histogram from). Can be re-run with different threshold parameters without re-computing scores. api_core/massing.py Stage 4. Reads the thresholding chain, builds floor plates with floor_plates.py, writes plates.json (world outlines), plates.obj (one closed prism per plate), the manifest, diagnostics and the run report with a Massing section. floor_plates.py Floor-plate massing geometry: base outline and facades split at corners, faces by nearest facade with squared corners, faces cut into square modules (along the facade and in depth), floor-by-floor module selection (tolerance, maximum volume, stacking, minimum width), plate outlines and closed prisms. api_core/exporting.py Stage 3. Loads the binary mask from Stage 2, removes small disconnected voxel clusters, reconstructs a triangle mesh (cubic voxel faces, or SDF-smoothed marching cubes with Taubin polishing), writes export.<format>, and writes run_report.md for the whole run. api_core/_stage_io.py The start and end of a stage (begin_stage, commit_manifest), manifest paths relative to the manifest's folder (stored_path) and reading an upstream manifest with its run ID check (load_upstream). api_core/_util.py Helpers shared by the stages: config resolution, device resolution ("auto" → "cuda" or "cpu"), JSON writing, reloading the occupancy grid, config snapshots. api_core/_diagnostics.py Writes each stage's diagnostic.json and, with diagnostic_plots, its plots (write_preprocessing_diagnostics, write_thresholding_diagnostics) after the stage's compute; score histograms, sky-patch hemisphere plots, the simple-vs-simulated weight comparison dome, score statistics, NaN/Inf issues. matplotlib loads when a plot is drawn. api_core/_reporting.py run_report.md generation.

docs.title: Geometry
docs.text: File Purpose surface_sampling.py Test-surface sampling. Discretizes each planar test-surface component into a regular grid of points with outward normals, projecting each face into its local 2D plane and using Shapely contains_xy for the in-polygon test; also computes the edge_taper weights and the analysis-mesh quads (AnalysisMesh). sample_surface is the preprocessing entry point. voxelization.py Converts a watertight mesh into a dense cubic boolean grid at the configured voxel_size, using the Warp parity voxelizer (voxelize_solid_warp, kernel in warp_kernels.py) (trimesh's rasterize-and-fill when Warp cannot run on the device) and filling enclosed cavities; the grid is cached in the active CarverSession. voxelize is the preprocessing entry point. meshing.py Mesh reconstruction. Removes small disconnected voxel clusters with scipy.ndimage.label and converts carved voxel masks back to triangle meshes, either as cubic voxel faces or through signed-distance-field smoothing, marching cubes, and Taubin polishing. finalize_mesh is the exporting entry point. io.py Mesh file I/O. load_mesh: reads a mesh through Trimesh (PLY, OBJ, STL...), rejects files without triangles, and runs fix_normals on meshes that are not watertight. save_mesh: writes a mesh; PLY files switch to double-precision vertices when float32 would round the coordinates, GLB files (save_glb) carry a whole-metre offset in their nodes, and STL files, float32 only, report a float32_coordinates issue when that rounds them by more than 1 mm. validate_inputs checks that the files a preprocessing run needs exist; load_meshes loads the maximum volume and the test surfaces and reports coordinates a float32 PLY file has rounded.

docs.title: Carving engines
docs.text: File Purpose carving.py The three carving strategies. carve_with_sun_rays (time-based): traces rays from test-surface points toward the sun positions of the analysis period and returns the carved grid and per-voxel hit counts. carve_with_sky_patch_rays (irradiance, benefit, daylight, radiative_cooling): traces rays toward the 145 Tregenza sky patches, weights each ray by its patch's mode-specific value, and returns the accumulated per-voxel scores. carve_with_planes (tilted_plane): traces one ray per sample point at the plane angle (per-octant angles supported) and removes every voxel at or above it in its column. column_postprocessing.py The column rules thresholding applies after the score threshold: carve_above_columns() and carve_above_scores() (the carve_above setting) and limit_column_slope() (max_slope_deg), as numba kernels. ray_tracing.py Ray generation and voxel traversal. trace_and_score_dda / trace_and_count_dda: launch the Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) kernels that step each ray through the voxel grid cell by cell and add the ray's weight (or a count of 1) to every voxel it crosses; they run on CUDA or on Warp's CPU backend, and there is no other tracer. follow_mass_behind_skin_dda: the skin rule. generate_sky_patch_rays / generate_sun_rays: expand sample points × directions into flat ray arrays, keeping only directions the surface faces. auto_batch_size: picks a ray batch size from the free GPU memory. warp_kernels.py Warp setup and every Warp kernel of the package (DDA traversal, skin rule, parity voxelizer), kept in one module so Warp compiles and caches them as one unit. dda_backend_available: whether the DDA backend can run on a device; require_dda_backend raises WarpBackendUnavailableError with the reason when it cannot. warmup_kernels: precompiles the kernels.

docs.title: Sky and sun models
docs.text: File Purpose sky_patches.py Tregenza hemisphere subdivision (145 patches) used by the weighted carving modes. fetch_tregenza_patch_directions: the 145 unit direction vectors. fetch_tregenza_patch_solid_angles: the solid angle (sr) of each patch. compute_EPW_based_weights: for irradiance and benefit, builds a Ladybug SkyMatrix (Perez all-weather model) from the EPW's direct-normal and diffuse-horizontal irradiance over the analysis period, each computation in a temporary folder of its own; benefit keeps only the hours below the balance point, or scales each hour by simulated weights. For daylight, returns the CIE standard overcast luminance distribution (brightest at the zenith, no EPW). compute_radiative_cooling_weights: long-wave cooling potential per patch from the Martin-Berdahl clear-sky emissivity with Bliss angular attenuation, for a horizontal surface; patches near the zenith get higher weights than those near the horizon. sun.py Solar position vectors. get_sun_vectors: uses Ladybug's Sunpath with the location from the EPW header to return unit vectors toward the sun for each sampled date-time of the analysis period (sun_steps_per_hour per hour), dropping positions below min_altitude and rotating by north_deg; time_basis says whether the date-times are local standard time, daylight saving time (one hour ahead) or true solar time. sample_period builds the analysis date/time list with Ladybug's AnalysisPeriod. weather_file.py read_weather_file: parses an EPW file with Ladybug once per path, modification time and size, and returns a ParsedWeatherFile that hands out copies (the location, the hourly dry-bulb temperatures, a Wea of the solar irradiance), so one caller's change cannot reach another. Used by the sun vectors, sky weights, cold period, simulated weights and the service's sun path. scoring.py Sky-patch weight dispatch and threshold selection. get_weights: calls the weighting function for the selected mode (Perez irradiance, heating benefit, CIE daylight, or radiative cooling). carve_fraction_threshold: the score cutoff above which the voxels hold a given fraction of the total score mass (two-pass weighted histogram, O(N)). headtail_threshold: Jiang (2013) head/tail breaks for heavy-tailed score distributions. Inside a CarverSession, get_weights is cached, keyed by every argument and by the contents of the EPW and simulated-weights files. simulated_weights.py Simulated benefit weights (opt-in via simulated_weights_path). Implements the ISO 13790 Annex C hourly thermal model ("5R1C": five conductances, one lumped mass capacitance, one zone) in NumPy, and derives the hourly marginal benefit/harm of solar gain by perturbation: for each hour of the year, one watt of solar gain is added and removed and the change in annual heating and cooling demand is attributed to that hour (benefit[t] / harm[t], both in [0, 1]; all 17,521 year-simulations, the base run plus two per hour, march as one vectorized batch). generate_simulated_weights: EPW + archetype → simulated_weights.json artifact with provenance metadata plus a .png heatmap preview. ZoneParams.from_archetype builds the thermal network from about 10 physical inputs; expand_shoebox derives all areas from a width/length/height + per-facade window-to-wall ratio shorthand. Validated against ETH's RC_BuildingSimulator (tests/data/oracle_5r1c_reference.json). Design note: design/simulated-weights.md.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: File Purpose mode_registry.py One ModeSpec per carving mode, in Grasshopper's menu order: whether it needs an EPW and an analysis period, its score kind (weighted_sum or violation_count), its weight unit, the mode-specific settings it reads, its description and its starting values (what differs from the schema defaults: analysis period, tilted-plane angle, carve fraction). Also MODE_ALIASES and canonical_mode_name(). Validation, the CLI schema command, the stages and the Grasshopper components read their mode facts from here. Standard library only. archetype_defaults.py The shoebox archetype defaults (ARCHETYPE_DEFAULTS, WINDOW_TO_WALL_DEFAULTS, ARCHETYPE_OPTIONAL_KEYS) read by usc archetype, simulated_weights.py and the USC_Archetype component. Standard library only. errors.py UrbanSolarCarverError and its subclasses ConfigError (with ConfigFieldError), InputError, StageChainError, MalformedEngineRequest and RunCancelled, plus UrbanSolarCarverWarning. Standard library only. run_context.py RunContext (issues, progress callback, cancel flag), Issue, report_issue(), report_progress() and run_context() / stage_context(). Standard library only. stage_settings.py The per-stage settings models (PreprocessingSettings, ThresholdingSettings, ExportingSettings, MassingSettings, RunOptions), stages_to_rerun() and stage_folder() (the one definition of the <run_folder>/<stage> layout). Does not import torch. load_config.py Reads a YAML configuration file and returns a validated UserConfig object. load_config: loads the YAML, expands an analysis_period: mapping, resolves relative paths against the YAML's folder, applies flat key=value overrides, and validates with Pydantic (all errors reported in one message). build_config: validates typed values (what a client holds) into a UserConfig and raises ConfigError with a ConfigFieldError per problem; load_config calls it. parse_override_value: converts override strings into Python values (booleans, None, JSON lists and objects, numbers). pydantic_schemas.py Data schemas. UserConfig: the Pydantic v2 model defining every pipeline parameter with types, defaults and value ranges (e.g. voxel_size must be 0.01-100); unknown keys are rejected. It normalizes threshold into a ThresholdSpec, checks mode requirements, and emits UrbanSolarCarverWarning for settings the mode ignores and when ray_batch_size is clamped. PreprocessingManifest / ThresholdingManifest: schemas for the JSON manifests written by the first two stages, so a later stage can be re-run from an earlier run's output.

docs.title: Infrastructure
docs.text: File Purpose compute_device.py The one rule for choosing the compute device. resolve_compute_device: auto/None picks CUDA when available, else the CPU; cpu, cuda, cuda:N and a torch.device are taken as given, and a CUDA choice without CUDA raises. warp_device_name: the Warp name of a torch device. Used by the stages, the session, the daemon, the weights, voxelization and the kernel launches. session.py Compute-session lifecycle. CarverSession: a long-lived object that keeps the CUDA context alive across pipeline calls and holds a value cache (voxelized grids, Tregenza patch directions and solid angles, and the sky-patch weights of the weighted modes). Keys cover the geometry, settings and device, so entries stay valid across runs; the cache holds at most 1 GiB (max_cache_bytes) and drops the least recently used entries beyond that. The daemon opens one session and keeps its cache between commands, returning only unused GPU memory after each; the Python API and CLI run without a session unless you open one (with CarverSession():). Compiled Warp kernels are cached by Warp itself, on disk. get_active_session: returns the session registered for a device, or None. session_cache: a decorator that stores a function's return value in the active session's cache under a key built from its arguments. engine_requests.py The request core every transport uses. parse_engine_request validates a message into a typed request (run, the stage commands, run_pipeline, simulate_weights, ping); config_for_engine_request builds its config from a YAML path or from the mode's starting values plus overrides; handle_engine_request runs it in a run context and returns a typed reply with the run's issues; answer_engine_message does all of this for dict transports and turns any failure into an error reply with error_type and, for config errors, config_errors. Does not import torch until a request runs. daemon.py Persistent background process for Grasshopper and the CLI's --daemon flag, a transport over engine_requests. serve: listens on 127.0.0.1 (localhost only) with Python's multiprocessing.connection, authenticated with a random key stored in ~/.urbansolarcarver/.daemon_authkey. Creates a CarverSession on startup and keeps it for the daemon's lifetime; each request goes to answer_engine_message, and only shutdown is handled by the daemon itself. Started and stopped with the CLI (urbansolarcarver daemon start/stop) or from Grasshopper with the USC_Session component. daemon_client.py The client side of the daemon, standard library only: the authkey file (resolve_daemon_authkey), the default host and port, and send_daemon_request. The CLI's daemon commands use it, so they do not load torch; the daemon reads its key through it too. carver_cli.py Command-line interface built with Typer, registered in pyproject.toml as both urbansolarcarver and usc. Commands: run (the sequencer, with --produce and --start-from), preprocessing, thresholding, exporting, massing (each with a config file -c, overrides -o, and optional --daemon), validate, schema (prints the config parameter table, filterable by --mode or --search), warmup, simulate-weights, archetype, ui (the browser interface) and daemon start/stop/status.

docs.title: Browser UI
docs.text:
File Purpose local_web_service/server.py The FastAPI application behind usc ui. create_app builds it; SecurityMiddleware refuses a Host header that is not the service's address and an API call or WebSocket without the launch token. Routes for projects, input files, settings, modes, examples, stage status, run summaries, result files, downloads and run events; serves the built front-end. Does not import torch. local_web_service/api_models.py The Pydantic models of the requests and replies; the front-end's types are generated from them. local_web_service/projects.py Project folders: name validation, the folder layout, project.json, uploads (several mesh files of a role are joined into one), config.yaml built from the settings the browser sends on top of the mode's starting values, and the voxel grid check. local_web_service/stage_records.py Which stages of a project are current, out of date or missing, and which stages a run has to execute. local_web_service/run_worker.py Runs a project in a background thread in two phases (analysis, then envelope and massing), publishes progress events and handles cancel. local_web_service/run_summary.py, score_points.py What the app shows of a run: the numbers of the carving and massing, the sun path and sky dome, and the scored voxels. local_web_service/gpu_warm_up.py Compiles the GPU kernels in the background at launch and reports the device or why the CPU is used. example_projects/ The three packaged examples (examples.json, mesh files and one weather file). ui_static/ The built front-end, committed. build_info.json holds a hash of the sources in app/.

app/ holds the front-end source (src/steps/ the six steps, src/settings_form/ the settings, src/viewer/ and src/viewer_overlays/ the 3D view, src/api_client/ the typed client). See Browser UI for building it.

docs.title: Simulated Benefit Weights
docs.text: Benefit mode's optional simulated weighting runs a small building simulation inside USC. A simulation brings physical assumptions that the geometric parts of USC do not have, so this page documents the engine, its origin, how it was validated, what the user supplies, and where its limits are.

docs.title: The engine
docs.text:
USC implements the ISO 13790 Annex C simple hourly method, commonly called the 5R1C model: a single thermal zone represented by five conductances and one lumped thermal-mass capacitance.

  • Nodes: outdoor air, supply air, indoor air, an internal surface node, and the thermal mass.
  • Conductances: ventilation, air-surface coupling, glazing, surface-mass coupling, and the opaque-envelope remainder, all derived per the standard (coupling coefficients h_is = 3.45 W/m²K, h_ms = 9.1 W/m²K, Λ_at = 4.5; thermal mass per ISO 13790 Table 12 mass classes).
  • Time stepping: Crank-Nicolson on the mass node, one hour per step, with the standard's three-step heating/cooling demand calculation (free-float, 10 W/m² test load, exact linear interpolation to the setpoint).

On top of the simulation sits perturbation attribution: for every hour of the year, the transmitted solar gain of that hour is perturbed by ±1 W and the change in annual heating and cooling demand is attributed to that hour (central differences). This yields two hourly series in [0, 1]:

Series Meaning benefit[t] fraction of a marginal joule of solar gain at hour t that offsets heating over the year harm[t] fraction that becomes cooling load

Attributing against the annual totals captures thermal lag: a noon gain stored in the mass and released into the cold evening still earns heating credit. All 17,521 year-simulations (the base run plus two per hour) run as one vectorized NumPy batch, in seconds.

docs.title: Origin and validation
docs.text:
The engine is an independent implementation, written directly from the ISO 13790 Annex C equation set in NumPy (urbansolarcarver/simulated_weights.py). It is not a fork, port, or adaptation of an existing simulator.

It is cross-validated against RC_BuildingSimulator, the ETH Zurich Architecture & Building Systems group's MIT-licensed implementation of the same annex (Jayathissa et al., "Optimising building net energy demand with dynamic BIPV shading", Applied Energy 202, 2017). The validation setup:

  • Three archetype scenarios: medium office, heavy masonry, light insulated.
  • Weather: the bundled Golden, CO TMY3 EPW (dry-bulb direct; transmitted solar from Ladybug's directional irradiance on each scenario's glazing, g = 0.6).
  • Compared quantities: annual heating and cooling demand totals (agreement to roughly 1 Wh/year, relative tolerance 1e-6), mean annual air temperature, and hourly air-temperature, mass-temperature, and heating/cooling-demand values at sampled hours across the year.
  • Method: the oracle's own derived conductances are fed into USC's engine directly, so the comparison isolates the hourly recurrence itself rather than parameter-derivation conventions (the two implementations intentionally differ on one of those: RC_BuildingSimulator uses U·A directly for the opaque-envelope conductance, USC applies the standard's serial split).
  • Artifacts: the oracle's driving arrays and reference outputs are committed verbatim in tests/data/oracle_5r1c_reference.json; the regression runs in the test suite on every change (tests/test_simulated_weights.py), deterministically, with no weather generation at test time.

Beyond the oracle comparison, the engine is checked for steady-state energy-balance closure against an independent hand-derived network reduction (constant outdoor temperature, no gains: demand converges to conductance × ΔT with the air node held at setpoint), and for the physical property that heavier mass classes flatten hour-to-hour mass-temperature variation.

Full derivation notes and the coefficient provenance live in the repository at design/simulated-weights.md.

docs.title: What you supply: the archetype
docs.text:
The archetype describes a typical building in about ten numbers. Two equivalent forms are accepted (configs/archetype_example.yaml shows both):

Shoebox form (areas derived for you):

Key Meaning width, length, height zone dimensions (m); floor area, volume, facade areas derived wwr window-to-wall ratio per facade, keyed north/east/south/west g_value glazing solar transmittance (applies to all windows) orientation optional rotation of the whole box, degrees clockwise from north

Explicit form: floor_area, volume, area_opaque, area_window, and a windows list of [azimuth_deg, area_m2, g_value].

Both forms additionally take: u_opaque, u_window (W/m²K), ach_vent, ach_infiltration (1/h), heat_recovery (0-1), mass_class (very_light … very_heavy, ISO 13790 Table 12), t_set_heating, t_set_cooling (°C), and internal gains as either a flat internal_gains_w_m2 (W/m², default 5) or a 24-value daily profile internal_gains_profile_w_m2.

Shading coefficients (optional, declared multipliers; no device geometry is modelled):

Key Meaning shading_permanent year-round solar transmission multiplier in [0, 1] (fins, context obstructions); 1 = no shading shading_hot additional multiplier applied only during hot_months (awnings, tents, seasonal vegetation); stacks with the permanent factor hot_months calendar months (1-12) when shading_hot is deployed, e.g. [6, 7, 8, 9]

Each coefficient accepts a scalar (all facades) or a per-facade mapping ({south: 0.8, west: 0.9}); windows are assigned to their nearest cardinal facade. The perturbation attribution is attenuated by the same factors, so the weights describe a marginal joule of exterior solar: a July joule arriving while the awning is out counts for little. The declared coefficients are recorded in the artifact's provenance. Note that a fixed overhang's blocking is concentrated in high-sun hours, so its effect is usually best expressed through shading_hot rather than shading_permanent.

The shipped example values are deliberately neutral, with no national defaults. For real projects, source values from TABULA (EU building-stock typologies), DOE prototype buildings (US), or your national code tables.

The usc archetype command builds and validates the file for you, printing the derived floor area, volume, and per-facade window areas so mistakes surface before any simulation runs:

usc archetype -o my_building.yaml -s width=12 -s wwr_south=0.4 -s mass_class=heavy
usc archetype --from my_building.yaml -o variant.yaml -s mass_class=light   # derive a variant

In Grasshopper, USC_Archetype assembles the archetype from five family feeder components (USC_ZoneGeometry / Fabric / Ventilation / Operation / Shading, one wire each), feeding USC_SimulateWeights, whose output path wires into USC_BenefitParams.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
The weights are a marginal, single-zone, schedule-free physical signal. They capture effects the binary balance-point rule cannot (thermal lag, mass state, gain saturation), but the model makes the following simplifications on purpose:

  • Single zone, lumped mass: the weights are facade-independent within an hour; time-of-day carries the directional signal. Perimeter-zone effects are out of scope for a massing tool.
  • Ideal, unlimited conditioning at the air node; continuous operation, no setback or occupancy schedules.
  • Fixed air-change rates: no night flushing, and no adaptive shading control. Without a declared shading_hot coefficient the harm channel is overstated, since real buildings have cheap defenses against summer sun that they lack for missing winter sun; declaring seasonal shading in the archetype makes harm a defensible estimate instead of a worst case. include_harm remains opt-in.
  • Flat internal gains, or one 24-hour profile repeated every day.
  • Marginal linearization: the weights describe one extra watt at the archetype's operating point; window sizes and g-values in the archetype set where gains saturate, and are recorded in the artifact's provenance metadata.
  • Unshaded derivation: the weights are computed for an unshaded archetype while the carve itself creates shading context; a first-order acceptable inconsistency for massing studies.
  • TMY weather; the ISO coupling coefficients carry the standard's residential-European calibration provenance.

Treat include_harm as a bracketing scenario

Without declared seasonal shading, harm is conservatively overstated (no night ventilation is modelled either), so the benefit-only weighting is the recommended default. Declaring shading_hot + hot_months in the archetype makes the harm channel a defensible estimate; even then, enable the subtraction deliberately for overheating-critical projects rather than as the standard mode.

docs.title: Traceability
docs.text: Every artifact records its full provenance (meta: method, EPW, the complete expanded archetype, perturbation size, timestamp), and every carve that consumes one records that provenance in its preprocessing diagnostics. The artifact file is read again on every preprocessing run, so a regenerated artifact takes effect on the next run. With diagnostic_plots: true, the run also writes a comparison dome quantifying how the simulated weights shifted the sky relative to the simple rule under the same configuration.
