docs.title: Running the tests
docs.text:
The Python suite (about 1330 tests in tests/) and the front-end suite (about 480 vitest tests in app/) run locally: there is no CI, because the engine runs on the GPU and hosted runners have none. Tests marked gpu are skipped automatically without CUDA.

Install the test dependencies once with pip install -e .[dev] (it includes pytest-xdist, which runs tests in parallel with -n). Run the commands below from the repository root with the repository's environment active. In a git worktree that has no environment of its own, put the worktree's sources first: PYTHONPATH=src python -m pytest ... (in PowerShell, $env:PYTHONPATH = "src" once).

docs.title: Four tiers
docs.text:
Times are wall times on an 8-core / 16-thread AMD Zen 2 with an RTX 3060, measured 2026-10-19.

Tier When Command Time 0 While editing python -m pytest tests/test_floor_plates.py -m "not slow" seconds 1 After every change python -m pytest -m "not slow" -n 8 about 45 s 2 Before each commit python -m pytest -m "not sweep" -n 8 about 65 s 3 Before merging python -m pytest -n 8 about 100 s

When app/ changed, also run the front-end checks of the same tier (see below): npm test takes about 12 s, npm run typecheck 5 s and npm run build 7 s.

docs.title: Tier 0: the files you are editing
docs.text:
Run the test file of the module you are changing, or one test with -k:

python -m pytest tests/test_floor_plates.py -m "not slow"
python -m pytest tests/test_floor_plates.py -k end_wings

--lf runs only the tests that failed last time, which is quick after a fix. In app/:

npx vitest run src/steps/ModeStep.test.tsx

docs.title: Tier 1: after every change
docs.text:
python -m pytest -m "not slow" -n 8

Leaves out the tests marked slow: end-to-end scenes, full-year simulations, sweeps and a real daemon process. When app/ changed, in a second terminal at the same time:

cd app
npm test && npm run typecheck

docs.title: Tier 2: before each commit
docs.text:
python -m pytest -m "not sweep" -n 8

Everything except the tests marked sweep (the 0.5 m floor-plate sweep and the Monte Carlo seeds). When app/ changed, rebuild the front end first: the pytest run includes the test that compares ui_static/build_info.json with the sources.

cd app
npm test && npm run build

npm run build runs the type check before it writes src/urbansolarcarver/ui_static/.

docs.title: Tier 3: before merging
docs.text:
python -m pytest -n 8

The whole suite, sweeps included. From time to time, and before a release, run it without -n (about 5 minutes): a serial run catches a test that only passes after another one has run. Also run, when they apply:

  • after a change to the engine's numerics, the randomised Monte Carlo sweep: python tests/montecarlo.py (see its docstring for the options);
  • after a change under grasshopper/components/, the Rhino smoke test tools/grasshopper_example_smoke_test.py (see Grasshopper);
  • before a release, the suite in a fresh install (see CONTRIBUTING.md, "Checking a fresh install").

docs.title: Markers
docs.text:
Marker Meaning Left out by slow Takes seconds: end-to-end scenes, simulations, a daemon process -m "not slow" sweep Exhaustive parameter sweeps and Monte Carlo seeds; always also slow -m "not sweep" gpu Needs a CUDA GPU; skipped automatically without one (automatic)

Mark a new test slow when it takes more than about a second, and sweep when it repeats a check over many parameter values that other tests already cover at a few chosen ones. pyproject.toml runs pytest with --strict-markers (a misspelt marker is an error) and --durations=15 (every run ends with its 15 slowest tests). After the run, tests/conftest.py also lists each test outside slow that took over 1 s; mark it slow or make it faster. Times grow by about half under -n 8, so a test listed only in a parallel run may be fine on its own.

An exact count in a test (panels, sample points, kept voxels of a packaged example) carries a comment on how to take the new value after a deliberate change of the example files or of the code that produces it.

docs.title: Running in parallel
docs.text: -n 8 starts 8 worker processes and hands out single tests to them; each worker pays about 8 s of imports and collection once. Tests must not depend on one another or on a shared file: each uses its own tmp_path. The engine computes each sky matrix in a temporary folder of its own, so workers computing sky matrices at the same time do not share Ladybug's weather folder. When another checkout is testing on the same machine at the same time, -n 4 leaves it room.

docs.title: Browser UI
docs.text: usc ui opens UrbanSolarCarver in your browser. You add the maximum volume and the test surfaces, choose a mode, run the analysis, adjust how much to carve while watching the result in 3D, build the envelope and building massing, and download the files. It runs the same engine as the CLI and the Python API; everything stays on your computer.

docs.title: Starting the interface
docs.text:
In the UrbanSolarCarver folder, double-click start-urbansolarcarver.bat on Windows, or run ./start-urbansolarcarver.sh in a terminal on Linux and macOS. The first time, the launcher installs UrbanSolarCarver with setup_env.py (this takes several minutes and needs Python 3.10 or newer); after that it starts the interface at once. A window stays open while the interface runs: close it (Windows) or press Ctrl+C (Linux, macOS) to stop UrbanSolarCarver. The launcher passes its arguments on to usc ui, so start-urbansolarcarver.bat --port 8780 works too. It uses the environment in .venv in the folder, or ~/.usc-venv when setup_env.py had to put it there; for an environment made with setup_env.py --venv-dir, set USC_VENV to that folder.

From a terminal with the environment active, the same command is:

usc ui

The command prints the address to open and opens it in your default browser once the service is listening. When another program already uses the port, the command says so and stops without opening the browser; choose a free port with --port. The address carries a token that is new on every launch, so keep using the page it opened (or the printed address) and not a bookmark from an earlier launch. Press Ctrl+C in the terminal to stop the service.

Option Default Meaning --port 8770 Port on 127.0.0.1 --projects-folder the folder chosen in the app, else ~/UrbanSolarCarver/projects Folder that holds one subfolder per project; it is created when missing. It wins over the folder chosen in the app for that launch --no-browser off Print the address without opening the browser --device, -d auto Compute device: auto, cpu or cuda

The browser interface is an optional extra of the package. setup_env.py installs it unless you pass --no-ui; to add it to an existing environment run python -m pip install -e ".[ui]" (see Installation). Without the extra, usc ui prints that command and exits, and every other command is unaffected.

When the service starts it compiles the GPU kernels in the background. The start screen shows "Preparing the GPU" until that ends; you can open a project and add files meanwhile, and the run buttons wait for the GPU.

docs.title: The start screen
docs.text:
The start screen shows the version, the device (the GPU's name, or that the CPU is used) and three cards:

  • New project: type a name (up to 64 letters, numbers, spaces, hyphens or underscores) and create the project.
  • Open a project: the projects folder, with Change folder, and the projects in it, newest first. Each project has a menu (see Managing a project).
  • Try an example: three projects with their files already in place, so you can run an analysis without preparing any input. Perimeter block (a perimeter block 126 by 92 m, mode Solar time-based) is the smallest, New building among neighbors (a plot of about 18 by 17 m among existing buildings, mode Solar energy) is the middle one, and District of many buildings (about 208 by 227 m, mode Solar energy) is the largest. The first time you choose an example, it makes a copy as a new project, so the example itself never changes. After that, choosing it opens that project again. A project records which example it came from, so it is found after a rename. To start from a fresh copy, use Reset to the example in the project's menu.

docs.title: The projects folder
docs.text:
Change folder opens the operating system's folder picker on this computer. The browser never sends a path: the service shows the picker and reads the folder you choose. The folder is remembered in ~/.urbansolarcarver/ui.json and used at the next launch. The projects already in the old folder stay there, and the list shows the projects of the new folder.

  • Change folder is offered on the start screen only, with no run active. While a run is active the start screen says the folder can be changed once the run has ended.
  • When the folder was given with --projects-folder, it wins for that launch and the start screen offers no Change folder. Start usc ui without the option to change it there.
  • When the folder picker cannot open (no display, or tkinter missing), the start screen says so and the old folder stays. The way that always works is to start with usc ui --projects-folder <folder>.

docs.title: Managing a project
docs.text:
Each project in the list, and the project name in the top bar, has a menu:

  • Open folder opens the project's folder in Explorer (Finder, or the file manager on Linux) on this computer. It works during a run.
  • Rename asks for a new name, checked by the same rule as a new project's name, and renames the folder.
  • Delete names the project and its folder and asks you to type the project name to confirm.
  • Reset to the example (projects made from an example) replaces the project's inputs, settings and results with a fresh copy of the example, after a confirmation. The project keeps its name.

Rename, delete and reset wait while the project's run is active.

Delete and Reset send the project folder to the recycle bin (Windows) or trash (macOS, Linux), so a mistake can be undone; UrbanSolarCarver does not delete it for good. They remove only that one project folder, and refuse when the folder is not a direct child of the projects folder, has no project.json of that project, or is or holds a symbolic link or junction. On Windows they work only for a folder on a fixed disk of this computer: on a network, removable or other drive they are refused, and you can delete the folder in the file manager. A folder larger than the recycle bin's size limit may be deleted for good by Windows, and the app cannot check this beforehand.

docs.title: The steps
docs.text:
A project opens as a list of six steps on the left, with the 3D view on the right. Each step shows a one-line summary when it is closed.

  1. Inputs. Drop or choose the maximum volume (the largest building you would allow), the test surfaces (the surfaces whose sun or sky the carving protects) and, for the modes that need one, a weather file (.epw). Meshes may be PLY, OBJ, STL or GLB; several files for one role are joined into one. The step lists each file with its triangle count and the size of all inputs together, and warns when the model looks as if it is not in meters.

  2. Mode. Six tiles in a grid of three by two, each with a coloured symbol and a plain name. The tile's tooltip holds a one-line description, what the mode needs and the engine name, for people who use the CLI.

    Tile Engine name What it does Angle rule tilted_plane Removes everything above a plane at a fixed angle from each facade Solar time-based time-based Keeps direct sun on the test surfaces during the hours you choose Solar energy irradiance Keeps sun and sky energy over the period Solar usefulness benefit Keeps sun in the hours that need heating Daylight daylight Keeps the view of an overcast sky Night cooling radiative_cooling Keeps a flat roof's view of the cold night sky. Experimental, and it assumes horizontal test surfaces

    Choosing a mode fills its starting values in Settings. Carving Modes explains the methods. 3. Settings. The analysis settings with plain labels, units and a help text for each: the analysis period, the mode's own settings and the detail (voxel size and, at the end of the detail settings, the rays per batch and the detailed statistics, which only change the run report). The sample spacing on the test surfaces, the grid margin and the ray length have no field: the engine's values apply (see below). The step shows the size of the voxel grid and refuses a grid larger than the analysis can handle, naming the smallest voxel size that fits. Run analysis is in this step. See Entering values. 4. Carving. How much to carve, with a histogram of the scores of the voxels (a log or linear scale) and the numbers of the last carving. In the weighted modes the Carving rule comes first: Manual (the Carve amount slider, in percent of the total score) or Automatic (no setting: the cut is found from the spread of the scores, and the step says where it fell). A cutoff on the scores that a config holds (from the command line or an earlier version) shows as Manual, at the carve amount it stands for. Solar time-based has a Shadow tolerated slider in m²·h; the Angle rule has no threshold. The histogram follows the control in both rules; the other carving settings (score smoothing, the cut above a carved voxel, the steepest step between columns) are folded at the end. Scores are in physical units: m²·h of shade (Solar time-based), kWh of solar energy or of useful solar heat a voxel blocks (Solar energy, Solar usefulness), and m² of fully hidden sky (Daylight, Night cooling); the histogram axis, the cutoff, the 3D legend and the slider ends say which. 5. Envelope and massing. Two parts that are built on their own, since the massing reads the carving and not the envelope. - Envelope: its settings (smooth surface, smoothing passes, the smallest pieces and fragments kept), Build envelope, and its result, the envelope volume (counted on the kept voxels the mesh was built from, after small pieces are dropped, not on the smoothed surface). - Building massing: its settings (ground floor and upper floor heights, grid module, permitted volume exceedance, whether floors rest on the floors below), Build massing, and its results: the gross floor area, the number of storeys and a table with the bottom, top and floor area of each storey.

    Each part has its own out-of-date mark, "Out of date for the current settings". The step's summary says what exists, for example "Envelope built, massing not built". A link at the bottom opens the run report. The grid module is the square module the storeys are built from and the narrowest piece of floor allowed. The permitted volume exceedance is the share of a module on a storey that may lie outside the carved envelope; the massing never leaves the maximum volume. Floor-plate massing describes the method. 6. Export. The mesh format of the carved envelope and the building massing, and the downloads: the carved envelope, the building massing, the building massing data (JSON), the settings (config.yaml) and the whole project as a zip. Each file is offered once it exists. The envelope and the massing are the files that were built, in the format they were built in. A change of format rebuilds the parts that exist (the envelope, the massing or both); while Carving is locked (see below), the format is stored without a build, Export says so, and the next build of each part writes the chosen format.

docs.title: Carving further with another criterion
docs.text:
The Export step's Carve further with another criterion makes the built envelope the project's maximum volume, so a second criterion carves what the first one kept. The result keeps only what every criterion in the chain keeps (the intersection of their envelopes). Each step voxelizes the envelope again on the new run's grid, so surfaces can move by up to about half a voxel per step. The order matters for settings that are a share of the current volume, such as carve_fraction.

The button asks once before it acts, and works only when the envelope is up to date with the settings. Then:

  • the envelope becomes the only maximum volume file, carved_envelope_1 (then _2, and so on), in the format it was exported in;
  • the files it replaces move to inputs/earlier_max_volumes/<step>/ in the project folder, so the maximum volume you started from is never lost;
  • project.json records each step in carving_chain: the mode and settings the envelope was carved with, when, and which files it replaced; the Inputs step shows the chain under the maximum volume ("Carved by Daylight, then Solar time-based");
  • the settings return to those of a new project, and the Mode step opens to choose the next criterion (when the default voxel size would make the grid too large, the voxel size the envelope was built with stays);
  • the test surfaces and the weather file stay; every result is out of date and the next run starts from the analysis.

docs.title: Entering values
docs.text:
A number with a range is entered with a slider and a number field side by side. The number field takes any value the engine accepts; the slider covers the range people normally use (for example 0.1 to 5 m for the voxel size). The balance temperature and the analysis period are strips with two handles instead, each handle with its exact value in a bubble over it, always shown; where the two handles are close, their bubbles move apart so they never overlap.

  • Balance temperature (Solar usefulness) is a strip from 10 to 30 °C, with a tick a degree and a label every 5 °C, and two handles, the two ends of the dead band, with the band between them filled. The lower end (named "Counts below" for a screen reader) is where sun starts to count: in hours colder than this. The upper end ("Too warm above") is where, with harm counted, hours warmer than this count against the sun. Each end moves on its own and cannot pass the other; the app sends the engine the middle as balance_temperature and half the width as balance_offset, the dead band the engine reads on both sides of the balance temperature. A press on the strip moves the nearer handle there, to the step of 0.5 °C; the arrow keys move a handle by 0.5 °C, Page Up and Page Down by 2 °C, Home and End to the ends of the strip. A value outside 10 to 30 °C (from a hand-edited config.yaml) pins its handle at the end of the strip, and its bubble shows the value. The lower handle comes first for Tab, as on the strip; where the two handles lie on one spot, the direction picks the end: a drag to the left or an arrow key toward the lower end moves the lower one, and to the right the upper one, the focus moving to that end's handle. Home or End on one spot take the lower or the upper end to the end of the strip.
  • Sample spacing on the test surfaces is not set in the browser: the engine samples them at half the voxel size, and a quiet line under Voxel size says so ("Test surfaces sampled every 0.5 m"). On the District example (Solar usefulness, 1 m voxels) half the voxel size differs from a 0.25 m reference in 0.9 % of the kept voxels, against 2.0 % for a spacing of 1 m, at about twice the analysis time (13.9 s against 7.1 s; 0.25 m takes 37 s). A project that stored a sample spacing (an earlier version let you set one) drops it when it opens, so its analysis shows as out of date once if that spacing was not half its voxel size. An analysis made before this change without a stored spacing sampled every 1 m, the old default, so it too shows as out of date once unless its voxel size is 2 m. In config.yaml, on the command line and in Grasshopper grid_step can still be set.
  • Units. Every number shows its unit beside the value: counts say what they count (Smoothing passes in passes, Rays per batch in rays, Cut voxels in voxels, Drop mesh fragments in faces), Sun positions per hour reads "12 per hour (every 5 minutes)", and only the Bliss constant, a number without a unit, has none.
  • Drop pieces smaller than is shown and typed in m³, though the engine stores min_voxels, a count of voxels: the form multiplies the count by the volume of a voxel at the voxel size it shows (300 voxels at 0.5 m read 37.5 m³) and turns a volume typed back into whole voxels, at least one. The stored count does not change when the voxel size does, so the volume shown follows the voxel size.
  • Grid margin (margin_frac) is hidden for now; the engine's default (1 % of the longest side) applies, or a value already in config.yaml.
  • Ray length (ray_length) has no field: rays stop where they leave the voxel grid, so the engine's default of 3000 m reaches across any grid at no cost. A value already in a project's config.yaml is kept and applies.
  • Edge strip with less weight (edge_taper) is shown in Night cooling only, under More mode settings: sample points closer than this to the edge of a test surface count less, from 0 at the edge to full at this distance, so a cooling street or courtyard does not clear the mass right beside it. 0 is off. The engine reads it in every weighted mode: a value already in a project's config.yaml is kept when the project opens, in any mode, and dropped when you choose a mode that does not show it.
  • Analysis period is one control with two strips.
    • The year strip has twelve months and two handles for the start and the end date, each with its date in a bubble ("21 Dec"). A period across the new year (start after end, as in October to April) is drawn wrapped.
    • The hour strip has two handles for the first and the last hour, each with its hour in a bubble ("10 h"). The last hour is inclusive, so 10 to 14 h samples 10:00 through 14:00. A range across midnight is drawn wrapped.
    • A drag is sent once, when you let go; a key or a preset is sent at once. The step summary writes the period in words ("21 Dec, 10 to 14 h"). A period not set yet says "Not set yet" under the strips.
    • Presets set the dates and keep the hours: 21 December, 21 June, Heating season and Whole year. The heating season follows the hemisphere of the weather file's latitude: 1 April to 31 October south of the Tropic of Capricorn (23.44 degrees), 1 October to 30 April elsewhere, within the tropics and without a weather file.
    • In Solar usefulness a fifth preset, Cold period from the weather file, sets the dates of the site's cold period: the longest run of days whose mean temperature over the month around them is below the balance temperature minus the dead band. Its tooltip, shown while the pointer is over the button or the keyboard focus is on it (Escape closes it), says what it found ("Cold period of the weather file, where the mean of the month around each day is below 13 °C: 30 Sep to 15 May."), or why it cannot be used yet: no weather file, no cold period in it, or a failure to read it. A screen reader reads the same text as the button's description. It needs the weather file. Changing the balance temperature later updates that text but not the dates already set; press the preset again to use the new ones. Solar usefulness already counts only the hours colder than that threshold, so the cold period mostly leaves out cold hours outside the heating season, such as cool summer mornings; it changes more when the experimental "include harm" option is on, whose warm hours depend on the period.
    • When you add or replace the weather file (not when a project opens with one), Settings shows one notice about the new file, with two buttons; either button closes it, and a later weather file replaces it. In Solar usefulness it offers the cold period of the new file when its dates differ from the period's, keeping the hours ("The new weather file (Brisbane, AUS) has its cold period from 3 May to 20 Sep; the analysis period is 30 Sep to 15 May.", Use the cold period or Keep); it waits for the cold period and shows nothing when the file has none. In Solar time-based and Solar energy it appears only when the new file is in the other hemisphere from the one before (a project without one counts as northern, as the starting values are), and offers the same dates six months on: the month plus six, the day held to the month's length, the last day of a month staying the last day (30 Apr gives 31 Oct). For example "The new weather file (Brisbane, AUS) is in the southern hemisphere: winter there is June to August. Shift the analysis period by six months, to 21 Jun, 10 to 14 h?", Shift by six months or Keep. A period that covers the whole year covers the same days six months on, so it gets no offer. A file within the tropics, or one whose latitude cannot be read, brings no offer, and the hemisphere of the file before it still counts for the next one. The offer is saved as any change of the period is; while a run is in progress the buttons are disabled, as the settings are. Either button moves the focus to the analysis period's start date. Once the period changes, by the button or by hand, the notice is gone and stays gone if the period is set back; choosing a mode without an analysis period (Angle rule, Daylight, Night cooling) dismisses it too. Screen readers announce the notice as it appears.
    • Each handle takes the keyboard: the arrow keys move it by one day or one hour, Page Up and Page Down by a month or six hours, Home and End to the first or last day or hour.
    • When the hours cross midnight on a single date, the end date moves to the next day ("21 to 22 Dec, 22 to 2 h"). A period stored earlier with one date and hours across midnight (an older save or a hand-edited config.yaml) is what the engine runs on every day of the year: the year strip is filled whole, the step summary reads "Every day, 22 to 2 h", and a note under the strips says so: "Every day, 22 to 2 h: the hours cross midnight on one date, which the engine runs on every day of the year. The next change makes it one night." The period is not written until you change it.

docs.title: Running: two phases
docs.text:
A run has two phases, so that the part that takes time happens once and the part you adjust is quick.

  1. Run analysis runs the sun analysis and the carving (the preprocessing and thresholding stages). The 3D view then shows the kept voxels coloured by score; the carved voxels are a separate layer, hidden at first, which the Layers menu shows. The progress shows the stages, the ray batches and the elapsed time, with a Cancel button.
  2. Build envelope and Build massing (in Envelope and massing) run on the voxel result you settled on in the Carving step: the exporting stage and the massing stage. Build envelope and massing in Carving builds both.

Between the two you change the threshold. The cutoff line on the histogram can be dragged in every rule, or moved with the keys of its handle (arrow keys a hundredth of the range, Page Up and Page Down a tenth, Home and End to the ends). While it moves, a line under the histogram previews the share of the volume the cut keeps, worked out in the browser from the voxel scores of the last carving, before the slope limit (the run gives the exact numbers); in the weighted modes it also gives the carve amount the cut stands for, which the slider shows. Letting go sets that carve amount (under Automatic it switches the rule to Manual, and the step says so), or in Solar time-based the cutoff itself, whose slider ends at the highest score the cutoff is compared with (after Remove everything above a cut), past which a cutoff carves nothing more. Choosing Manual starts from the amount the cut on the histogram carves. Moving the slider or typing a value moves the line too. Update carving applies the change, which thresholds the scores again without repeating the analysis; until then the line stays where it was set, drawn in the accent colour as a preview. Switching on Update when I change the threshold applies each change as you let go of the line or the slider or leave the field. The choice is remembered per project in the browser.

The interface keeps track of what each result was built from. When you change a setting or an input after a result exists, that result stays visible, dimmed and labelled out of date, and the step that needs a run says so. While a dimmed result is shown in the 3D view, an Out of date stamp sits at the top of the view (Updating while a run replaces it); it has nothing to click and goes once the results are current. Running again replaces it. A run only starts the stages whose results are missing or out of date.

While the mode or the analysis settings in the form differ from the stored ones, Carving is locked, because a build would have to run the analysis first. The two builds then wait with a message to run the analysis again, and a mesh format change is stored and written by the next build of each part.

docs.title: The 3D view
docs.text:
The view has a compass, an axis gizmo (the three lettered axes, drawn straight on the viewport) and a legend for the coloured layers. The Layers menu switches the maximum volume, the test surfaces, the kept and carved voxels, the sun path, the sky dome, the carved envelope and the building massing. Buttons frame the whole model, show the top view and switch between a light and a dark viewport (remembered in the browser).

The ground aid button cycles through three states: off, a ground grid with a scale bar, and a compass ring on the ground around the scene (ticks every 10 degrees, the letters N, E, S and W every 90 degrees, rotated by the north direction). The button names the aid it switches to, and the choice is remembered in the browser. The compass ring, the sun path and the sky dome are centred on, and sized to, everything loaded (the maximum volume and the test surfaces together).

docs.title: Where projects are kept
docs.text:
Each project is a folder in the projects folder:

<projects folder>/<project name>/
├── inputs/        The files you added (max_volume/, test_surfaces/, weather.epw)
│                  and the joined meshes the engine reads (joined/)
├── config.yaml    The settings, a normal USC configuration file
├── project.json   The project's record: the files you added with their triangle counts, the input revision,
│                  the example it came from (if any)
│                  and one record per completed stage (with the settings that stage ran with)
└── run/           The engine's output: preprocessing/, thresholding/, exporting/ and massing/

config.yaml works outside the interface: its paths are relative to the project folder, so usc run -c <project folder>/config.yaml runs the same analysis from the command line. Thresholding also writes scores_compared_with_cutoff.npy in its folder (the values the cutoff is applied to, which the histogram draws). To delete a project, use Delete in its menu (see Managing a project), or delete its folder in the file manager.

docs.title: Security
docs.text: The service listens on 127.0.0.1 only and checks the Host header of every request, which stops a web page on another site from reaching it. Every request to the API needs the token of the launch, which only the printed and opened address carries, and the service takes no file path from the browser: it derives every folder from a validated project name, and the folder picker is shown by the service on this computer.

docs.title: Without a CUDA-enabled GPU
docs.text: When no CUDA-enabled GPU is found, the start screen says so and the engine runs on the CPU. The results are the same, and an analysis takes noticeably longer, so start with a larger voxel size or with the smallest example. --device cpu chooses the CPU even when a GPU is present.

docs.title: Rebuilding the front-end after changing app/
docs.text:
The interface is a React and three.js application whose source is in app/. The package carries its built files in src/urbansolarcarver/ui_static/, so using usc ui needs no Node.js. After changing app/:

cd app
npm install
npm run typecheck  # tsc --noEmit: the type check alone
npm run build      # runs the type check first, then writes src/urbansolarcarver/ui_static/ and build_info.json
npm test           # the front-end tests

A type error stops npm run build before anything is written.

Commit the rebuilt ui_static/ with the source change: a test compares the hash in build_info.json with the sources and fails when they differ.

If the service's API changed, regenerate the client types with npm run api-types. It runs python with the ui extra installed, so activate the repository's environment first (in a git worktree without an environment, set PYTHONPATH=../src and use a Python that has the extra).

docs.title: Carving
docs.text:
The carving module implements the three geometric strategies used to remove voxels from the maximum buildable volume:

  • Sun-ray carving (carve_with_sun_rays): traces rays along actual sun vectors at specific dates/times. Used by the time-based mode.
  • Sky-patch carving (carve_with_sky_patch_rays): traces rays toward Tregenza sky patches weighted by irradiance, heating benefit, daylight luminance, or radiative cooling potential. Used by the irradiance, benefit, daylight, and radiative_cooling modes.
  • Plane carving (carve_with_planes): removes voxels above a tilted cut plane at a fixed angle from each test surface. Used by the tilted_plane mode.

All three take a voxel grid and surface sample points with normals. Sky-patch carving returns per-voxel weighted scores; sun-ray and plane carving return a carved grid and, on request, per-voxel hit counts. The preprocessing stage stores these as scores.npy (for time-based, the counts are converted to m²·h), and the thresholding stage turns them into a binary carving mask.

docs.title: UrbanSolarCarver: carving utilities
docs.text:
Purpose

Convert point/normal samples on analysis surfaces into ray sets, trace those through a voxelized envelope, and count or score the voxels they visit. Supports:

• Time-based solar carving (sun vectors from the EPW for specific datetimes): every visited voxel is removed. • Sky-patch-weighted carving (Tregenza patches + mode-specific weights): returns per-voxel scores; the threshold is applied later, in api_core/thresholding.py. • Tilted-plane daylight carving (single or per-octant plane angle): every voxel at or above a visited voxel in its column is removed; extra rays rotate the plane around convex turns of the test-surface outline.

Raytracing contract

Rays are traced by the fused DDA kernels of warp_kernels.py (launched from ray_tracing.py), which visit every voxel a ray crosses exactly once and accumulate counts or scores in place; without Warp the carvers raise WarpBackendUnavailableError. The kernels count voxels that lie entirely in front of the surface a ray starts from, plus the surface's skin voxels (crossed by its plane) that are occupied and have nothing of the max volume behind them. Occupied skin voxels with max volume behind them are the surface's own skin: not counted, but raised to the value of the voxel behind them once tracing is done (_follow_mass_behind_skin), so they never outlast the mass behind them.

Coordinate/scale conventions

grid_origin is the world-space min corner for grid index [0,0,0]. grid_extent is the physical cube size (meters). grid_resolution is D, the number of voxels per side, so one voxel is grid_extent / D meters wide. The tracers receive scale = grid_extent.

Determinism and batching

Given a fixed config, hit counts are deterministic. Float scores are summed with atomic adds on the GPU, so the order of additions, and therefore the last bits of a score, can differ between runs. Rays are processed in batches of the ray_batch_size run option (0 = sized from free GPU memory) on the device of the input voxel grid.

docs.title: carve_with_sun_rays(voxel_grid, grid_origin, grid_extent, grid_resolution, sample_points, sample_normals, settings, datetimes, return_counts=False, return_rays=False, *, ray_batch_size)
docs.text:
Time-based carving of a voxel grid with sun vectors for explicit datetimes.

This builds a classical solar envelope by tracing rays toward the sun positions computed from the EPW location for the given datetimes. No scoring, normalization, or thresholding is applied here: any voxel visited by any ray is removed from the returned grid.

Core procedure 1. Compute sun vectors for the provided datetimes from the EPW file and drop those below settings.min_altitude. 2. For each surface sample point, build rays toward the sun directions on the outward side of its normal (dot product > 0). 3. Trace each ray through the grid (exact Warp DDA when available), counting hits per voxel and skipping voxels behind the source surface. 4. Remove every voxel visited by at least one ray.

docs.text:
Score each voxel by the sky-patch weight of the rays that cross it.

Each Tregenza sky patch gets a weight according to settings.mode: • irradiance: cumulative direct + diffuse irradiance per patch (kWh/m²) from the EPW over the analysis hours (Ladybug sky matrix). • benefit: the same, counted only in hours cold enough for solar gains to offset heating (kWh/m²), optionally minus hot-hour irradiance (include_harm). • daylight: relative luminance of the CIE standard overcast sky times the patch solid angle. • radiative_cooling: long-wave cooling potential from the dew point and the Bliss angular law, normalized to sum to 1.

Procedure: 1. Take the 145 Tregenza patch directions. 2. Cast a ray from each sample point toward every patch on the outward side of its normal. 3. Trace the rays through the voxel volume and add each ray's patch weight (times its point weight, if given) to every voxel it visits in front of its source surface.

No voxel is removed here: thresholding the scores into a keep/carve mask happens in api_core.thresholding.

docs.title: carve_with_planes(voxel_grid, grid_origin, grid_extent, grid_resolution, sample_points, sample_normals, settings, return_counts=False, *, ray_batch_size)
docs.text:
Tilted-plane daylight carving.

One ray per sample point: 1) Project the surface normal onto the XY plane to get n_xy. 2) Select the tilt angle α (single value or per-octant table). 3) Form d = cos(α)·n_xy + sin(α)·ẑ and trace a ray along it. Every voxel at or above a visited cell in its (x, y) column is deleted: the ray traces the plane's section through that column, and everything above the plane is forbidden, not only the cells the ray crosses.

Where the test-surface outline turns convexly (two panels meeting at an outside corner or a kink), the rays of the two panels diverge. Extra rays from the corner sweep the headings between the two normals, so the plane rotates around the corner instead of leaving the columns between the diverging rays standing (see :func:_corner_fan_rays).

See :func:carve_with_sun_rays for shared parameter descriptions.

required settings PreprocessingSettings

Must contain tilted_plane_angle_deg: a single angle in degrees above the horizon, or an 8-element list [N, NE, E, SE, S, SW, W, NW] looked up by the compass direction the surface faces (which uses north_deg).

required return_counts bool

If True, return a 4th element: per-voxel counts, propagated up each column (a voxel's count is the largest ray count at or below it).

False ray_batch_size int

Rays processed per batch (0 = automatic); keyword only.

required

The sample points (one ray each; the corner rays are not included).

docs.title: Column post-processing
docs.text: column_postprocessing.py holds the column rules thresholding applies after the score threshold: carve_above_columns (the carve_above setting), carve_above_scores (for each voxel, the score cutoff below which carve_above removes it; thresholding uses it so that carve_fraction counts what carve_above removes) and limit_column_slope (the slope limit, max_slope_deg).

docs.title: urbansolarcarver.column_postprocessing
docs.text:
UrbanSolarCarver: column post-processing of the carved grid

Column rules applied by thresholding after the score threshold, so the kept volume is a buildable height field:

  • carve_above_columns / carve_above_scores: carve every occupied voxel above the lowest sufficiently-carved region of each (x, y) column (carve_above, carve_above_min_consecutive), on a boolean carve mask or directly on the scores.
  • limit_column_slope: cut columns that rise more steeply than max_slope_deg above a median-filtered height map, which turns one-voxel spires and tall cliffs into ramps. It only removes voxels.

The column loops are numba kernels.

docs.title: carve_above_columns(mask, voxel_grid, min_consecutive=1)
docs.text:
Carve occupied voxels above the lowest sufficiently-carved run per column.

For each (x, y) column, scans bottom-to-top (z=0 upward) for runs of consecutive carved voxels (occupied in voxel_grid, False in mask; empty cells break a run and never count as carved):

  • Runs with length >= min_consecutive trigger carve-above: all occupied voxels above the run are carved. The first (lowest) qualifying run triggers; scanning stops for that column.
  • Shorter runs do not trigger, but stay carved: the result only ever removes voxels, so it never re-violates the carving constraint.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default mask ndarray (D, D, D) bool

Thresholding mask. True = keep, False = carved. Not mutated.

required voxel_grid ndarray (D, D, D) bool

Original envelope occupancy. True = occupied.

required min_consecutive int

Minimum consecutive carved voxels to trigger carve-above.

1

Returns:

Type Description ndarray (D, D, D) bool

A copy of mask with the occupied voxels above qualifying runs set to False.

docs.title: carve_above_scores(scores, occupancy, min_consecutive=1)
docs.text:
For each voxel, the score cutoff below which carve_above removes it.

Carving the occupied voxels that score above a cutoff t and then running :func:carve_above_columns removes exactly the occupied voxels whose value here is above t: a voxel goes when it scores above t itself, or when some run of min_consecutive consecutive occupied voxels below it in its column all score above t. So the value is the larger of the voxel's own score and, over those runs below it, the smallest score in the run. Empty cells break runs.

With these values a score-mass cutoff can count everything carve_above removes, not only the voxels the cutoff picks itself. NaN scores count as +inf (always carved).

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default scores ndarray (X, Y, Z) float required occupancy ndarray (X, Y, Z) bool required min_consecutive int 1

Returns:

Type Description ndarray (X, Y, Z) float64

Values on empty cells are their own score and carry no meaning.

docs.title: limit_column_slope(mask, occupancy, max_slope_deg, median_size=5)
docs.text:
Lower columns that rise too steeply above their neighbours.

Each building column's kept height (one above its highest kept voxel, 0 if nothing is kept) is capped so that it rises at most tan(max_slope_deg) voxels per voxel of horizontal distance above a reference height map, counting the reference at the column itself as one voxel away; every kept voxel above the cap is removed. The result only ever removes voxels.

The reference is the kept height map after a median_size x median_size median filter over the building's columns, so features one or two columns wide are ignored: a single tall column (a spire) is measured against its surroundings and ends at most one slope step above them, and a single low column (a stub left at a curved edge) or a narrow slot does not pull its neighbours down. Wider differences in height, including next to areas carved to the ground, become ramps of the given slope, cut from the taller side. Columns outside the building (no occupied voxel) take no part.

The cap never rises when the input loses voxels, so carving more before this step never keeps more after it (a carve_fraction slider stays nested).

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default mask ndarray (X, Y, Z) bool

Kept voxels (True), normally after carve_above. Not mutated.

required occupancy ndarray (X, Y, Z) bool

The building's voxels before carving; decides which columns count.

required max_slope_deg float

Steepest allowed rise between neighbouring columns, in degrees above horizontal (0 < angle < 90; voxels are cubes, so the slope is the same in metres).

required median_size int

Width in voxels of the median filter that builds the reference.

5

Returns:

Type Description ndarray (X, Y, Z) bool

A copy of mask with the voxels above each column's cap removed.

docs.title: CLI
docs.text:
Command-line interface built with Typer, installed as urbansolarcarver and its short alias usc. Provides the same 3-stage pipeline as the Python API, plus daemon management, config validation and introspection, and the simulated-weights tools.

# Run the whole pipeline
urbansolarcarver run -c config.yaml

# Produce the floor plates too, or reuse the scores and re-threshold
urbansolarcarver run -c config.yaml --produce exporting --produce massing
urbansolarcarver run -c config.yaml --start-from thresholding -o carve_fraction=0.5

# Run pipeline stages
urbansolarcarver preprocessing -c config.yaml
urbansolarcarver thresholding  -c config.yaml -f outputs/preprocessing/manifest.json
urbansolarcarver exporting     -c config.yaml -f outputs/thresholding/manifest.json

# Override any config value on the fly
urbansolarcarver preprocessing -c config.yaml -o voxel_size=0.5 -o mode=irradiance

# Check a config without running anything
urbansolarcarver validate -c config.yaml

# Build and validate a building archetype (prints derived areas)
urbansolarcarver archetype -o my_building.yaml -s width=12 -s wwr_south=0.4 -s mass_class=heavy

# Generate simulated benefit weights (writes simulated_weights.json + .png preview)
urbansolarcarver simulate-weights -e weather.epw -a my_building.yaml

# List the config parameters (optionally --mode benefit or --search threshold)
urbansolarcarver schema

# Precompile the Warp kernels
urbansolarcarver warmup

# Daemon lifecycle
urbansolarcarver daemon start
urbansolarcarver daemon status
urbansolarcarver daemon stop

Without -f, thresholding and exporting look for the previous stage's manifest.json under the config's out_dir.

run takes --produce (repeatable; preprocessing, thresholding, exporting or massing; default exporting) and runs the stages those need. --start-from (default preprocessing) skips the stages before it and reads their output from <out>/<stage>. Both work with --daemon, which sends the daemon's run command.

Issues noticed during a command (settings the mode ignores, nothing carved, ...) print after the result under Issues: as stage: code: message. A package error (an invalid config, an unusable input file, a missing or stale upstream output) prints Error: <message> and exits with 1, without a traceback.

docs.title: urbansolarcarver.carver_cli
docs.text:
UrbanSolarCarver command-line interface.

Exposes the pipeline stages (preprocessing, thresholding, exporting, massing) as individual subcommands, plus run, which runs the stages needed for what --produce asks for (the carved mesh by default). Performance evaluation is out of scope: use Ladybug/Honeybee/Radiance on the exported mesh.

Utility commands: - warmup: precompile the Warp kernels once so the first run is not slow. - simulate-weights: build a simulated-weights file for benefit mode. - archetype: write and check a shoebox archetype YAML for simulate-weights. - validate: load and validate a YAML config without running anything. - schema: print a filterable parameter reference (by mode or keyword). - daemon: start / stop / status of the persistent GPU daemon used by Grasshopper and the --daemon flag on pipeline commands.

Design decisions ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ All heavy imports (torch, warp, api_core) are deferred to function bodies so that lightweight commands (--help, schema, validate, daemon) start quickly without initialising CUDA or compiling Warp kernels. Pipeline commands import urbansolarcarver.api inside their bodies, and the daemon commands use the standard-library daemon_client.

The --daemon flag on each pipeline command sends the job to a running daemon over localhost TCP (multiprocessing.connection), sharing the same RPC mechanism used by the Grasshopper plugin.

docs.text:
Compile the Warp compute kernels ahead of time.

Warp compiles kernels just in time on first use, a one-time cost of roughly 3-10 s per machine, device and code version that is cached on disk afterwards. Run this once after installing or updating UrbanSolarCarver so the first carving run reflects real compute time. (setup_env.py and the daemon do this automatically.) Exits with code 1 if the Warp backend is not available on the device.

docs.title: simulate_weights(epw=Option(..., '-e', '--epw', exists=True, readable=True, help='EPW weather file'), archetype=Option(..., '-a', '--archetype', exists=True, readable=True, help='Archetype YAML (see configs/archetype_example.yaml)'), out=Option(Path('simulated_weights.json'), '-o', '--out', help='Output artifact path'), eps=Option(1.0, '--eps', help='Perturbation size in W (central differences)'))

Write a simulated-weights file for benefit mode.

Runs the ISO 13790 Annex C simple hourly model (5R1C: five resistances, one capacitance) for the archetype and weather file, perturbs the solar gain by +/- eps W each hour, and records the hourly marginal benefit and harm of solar gain (central differences).

The file is read through benefit mode's simulated_weights_path config key, where it replaces the balance-point on/off hour filter with these hourly weights. See design/simulated-weights.md.

Build a shoebox archetype, validate it, and report derived quantities.

The file is validated through the same code path the generator uses (expand_shoebox + ZoneParams.from_archetype) before writing, and the derived floor area, volume, and per-facade window areas are printed so mistakes surface here rather than inside a simulation.

Only the shoebox form is built by this command; explicit-area archetypes are edited directly in YAML (see configs/archetype_example.yaml).

Exits with code 1 if the config fails schema or value checks. Missing mesh, EPW and simulated-weights files, and a simulated-weights file that cannot be read, are printed as warnings only (exit code 0). Does not initialise CUDA or import torch.

The service listens on 127.0.0.1 only. Each launch creates a random token, which the browser receives once in the address and sends with every request; the address is printed here as well. The compute kernels are compiled in the background while the interface is used. Press Ctrl+C to stop.

Does nothing if a daemon already answers on the port. docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
USC uses YAML files for all pipeline parameters. The configuration system provides:

  • Typed values through build_config, for clients that hold values rather than a file (Grasshopper through the daemon).
  • YAML loading of a flat mapping of settings; an analysis_period: mapping with Ladybug AnalysisPeriod.to_dict() keys is expanded into the six period fields. Relative paths are resolved against the YAML file's folder.
  • Overrides (-o key=value on the CLI, or a mapping in Python) that replace top-level values from the file.
  • Pydantic v2 validation with value ranges, type coercion, rejection of unknown keys, and one error message listing every problem. Both entry points raise ConfigError, whose errors list gives the field and message of each problem.
  • Manifest schemas for the preprocessing and thresholding stages, so a later stage can be re-run from an earlier run's output.

See also: Configuration guide for the user-facing parameter reference.

docs.text:
Load a YAML config, apply overrides, and validate it into a user_config.

Overrides come from the CLI (key=value strings), the daemon, or Grasshopper. :func:build_config validates already-typed values (no YAML involved) and raises a structured :class:~urbansolarcarver.errors.ConfigError. The schema itself lives in :mod:pydantic_schemas.

docs.title: parse_override_value(raw)
docs.text:
Convert a key=value override's value into a Python value.

"true"/"false" become bool and "null"/"none" None (case-insensitive); JSON lists and objects are parsed ([45,40,35]), then int, then float; anything else stays a string. "inf" and "nan" stay strings so the schema reports them clearly.

parse_override_value("true") True parse_override_value("3.5") 3.5 parse_override_value("foofoo") 'foofoo'

docs.title: Mode starting values
docs.text: mode_registry.MODES holds one ModeSpec per carving mode. Its starting_values are the settings that differ from the schema defaults and fill a new config for the mode: the analysis period of time-based, irradiance and benefit, tilted_plane_angle_deg: 45 for tilted_plane and carve_fraction: 0.35 for radiative_cooling. A client with no YAML file (Grasshopper through the daemon's run command) gets its config from these values plus its overrides. The schema defaults and validation rules are unchanged, so a CLI config without carve_fraction keeps 0.7 in every mode and time-based still requires an analysis period. The files in configs/ repeat the starting values as commented examples. ModeSpec.description is the text the Grasshopper mode component shows, MODE_ALIASES lists the accepted spellings (time_based, tilted-plane, ...) and canonical_mode_name(name) maps a name to the canonical one.

docs.title: urbansolarcarver.pydantic_schemas
docs.text:
Pydantic schemas for YAML configuration validation and stage manifests.

Defines :class:UserConfig (the pipeline configuration model, imported elsewhere as user_config), :class:ThresholdSpec (the normalized threshold setting), the four stage manifest schemas (:class:PreprocessingManifest, :class:ThresholdingManifest, :class:ExportingManifest, :class:MassingManifest) and the project-specific warning class :class:UrbanSolarCarverWarning.

The config schemas use extra='forbid' so that typos in YAML keys are caught at load time rather than silently ignored. The manifest schemas use Pydantic's default and ignore unknown keys.

hold value (0-1) of the total score mass.

* ``headtail``: head/tail breaks * ``cutoff``: carve voxels scoring strictly above ``value``; for

Raises ValueError if analysis_period is not a mapping, has an unknown key, or disagrees with a flat period field in the same dict.

docs.title: Daemon
docs.text:
A persistent background process that keeps a CarverSession (and with it the CUDA context and the compiled Warp kernels) alive for low-latency calls from Grasshopper or other clients. It communicates via Python's multiprocessing.connection over localhost; clients authenticate with a random key stored in ~/.urbansolarcarver/.daemon_authkey.

The daemon is started and stopped via the CLI (urbansolarcarver daemon start/stop, daemon status to check it) or from within Grasshopper using the USC_Session component. It binds to 127.0.0.1 only and is not reachable from the network.

docs.title: A transport over the engine requests
docs.text:
The daemon only carries messages. Each request is a dict with a cmd key; the daemon passes it to engine_requests.answer_engine_message, which runs it and returns the reply dict, with status "ok" or "error". The commands, their keys and their replies are described in Engine requests. The daemon itself handles one more command, shutdown, which stops it.

Clients reach it through daemon_client.py, which uses only the standard library: resolve_daemon_authkey reads (or creates) the key and send_daemon_request sends one request, so asking the daemon something does not load torch. Grasshopper keeps its own copy of the key reading in usc_gh.py, because Rhino's Python does not import this package.

A message the daemon cannot unpickle gets an error reply too, and the daemon keeps running. Failed requests are logged with their traceback in the daemon's console or log file.

docs.title: urbansolarcarver.daemon
docs.text:
Long-running server that keeps a GPU session alive between pipeline calls.

Used by the Grasshopper components and the CLI --daemon flag. Starts a single CarverSession and listens on a multiprocessing.connection Listener for request dicts such as {"cmd": "run", "produce": [...], ...}. The daemon is a transport: each request goes to :func:urbansolarcarver.engine_requests.answer_engine_message, which runs it and returns the reply dict ("status" is "ok" or "error") that is sent back. Only shutdown is handled here, since it stops the transport.

Security assumptions
  • Localhost only: the daemon binds to the loopback interface. Host names that do not resolve to 127.0.0.1 or ::1 are rejected at startup.
  • Authkey: 32 random bytes, stored as 64 hex characters in ~/.urbansolarcarver/.daemon_authkey, are generated on first use. Clients must present this key.
  • Pickle IPC: multiprocessing.connection uses pickle internally. Any process that holds the authkey can execute arbitrary code in the daemon's context. This is acceptable because both endpoints run on the same machine under the same user account.
  • Not designed for multi-user or server deployment. Do not expose the daemon port to a network.

docs.title: serve(address, authkey, device_arg='auto')
docs.text:
Serve pipeline requests from Grasshopper and the CLI until "shutdown".

Keeps one CarverSession (CUDA context and compiled Warp kernels) alive across requests. The commands are those of :mod:engine_requests, plus shutdown. Requests are handled one at a time; a failing request becomes an error reply and the server keeps running.

docs.title: Engine requests
docs.text:
urbansolarcarver.engine_requests turns a request message into an engine call and a reply. Every transport uses it: the daemon today, a local HTTP service later. It does not import torch until a request runs.

  • parse_engine_request(message) validates a dict into one of the request models below, or raises MalformedEngineRequest (a ValueError) when the message is not a dict, names an unknown command, or lacks or misuses a key.
  • config_for_engine_request(request) builds the config: from the YAML file in config with overrides on top, or, without a file, from the starting values of the mode the overrides name (load_config.build_config_from_mode_starting_values).
  • handle_engine_request(request, session, context=None) runs the request inside a run context and returns a reply model; engine errors propagate. A given RunContext receives progress, issues and cancellation.
  • answer_engine_message(message, session) does all of this for transports that carry dicts and never raises: any failure becomes an error reply.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
run runs the stages needed to produce produce, through the same sequencer as run_pipeline().

Request key Meaning produce List of stages to produce: preprocessing, thresholding, exporting, massing run_folder The folder that holds one subfolder per stage start_from First stage to run (default preprocessing); earlier stages are read from run_folder config Optional path of a YAML config overrides Optional list of key=value strings, or a mapping

Without config, the config is built in memory from the starting values of the mode named in the overrides (mode is required) with the overrides on top; no file is written.

The reply holds stage_folders (stage name to folder, only for the stages that ran in this call), manifest (the manifest of the last of them), issues, and export_path (exporting), plates_path, mesh_path (the OBJ) and export_mesh_path (the plates in final_mesh_format) (massing) for the stages that produced them.

They need config; every stage but preprocessing also needs from, the upstream stage's folder or manifest. out_dir defaults to <config out_dir>/<stage>. The reply has issues and manifest, export_path (exporting) or plates_path, mesh_path and export_mesh_path (massing).

run_pipeline runs preprocessing, thresholding and exporting into out_dir (default: the config's out_dir); Grasshopper definitions saved before run existed still send it. simulate_weights writes a simulated-weights file (epw, archetype, out, optional internal_gains_w_m2 and eps) and replies with artifact and preview. ping replies with the process id (pid).

docs.text: Every reply to a run or stage command has issues, a list of {stage, code, message}. An error reply has error (the text), error_type (the exception class name; MalformedEngineRequest for a malformed request) and, for a ConfigError, config_errors, a list of {field, message}.

docs.title: urbansolarcarver.engine_requests
docs.text:
Requests the engine answers, shared by every transport.

A transport (the pickle daemon today, an HTTP service later) receives a message; this module turns it into an engine call and a reply:

  • :func:parse_engine_request validates a message into one of the request models, or raises :class:~urbansolarcarver.errors.MalformedEngineRequest.
  • :func:config_for_engine_request builds the request's config: from its YAML file with the overrides on top or, without a file, from the starting values of the mode the overrides name.
  • :func:handle_engine_request runs a request inside a run context and returns a reply model; engine errors propagate to the caller.
  • :func:error_reply_for turns an exception into an error reply.
  • :func:answer_engine_message does all of this for transports that carry plain dicts, and never raises.

Stopping a transport is the transport's own business, not a request here. Importing this module does not import torch: the stage functions are imported when a request runs.

docs.title: Geometry
docs.text:
The geometry pipeline from raw meshes to the output mesh, in three modules:

  1. Surface sampling (surface_sampling.py): discretizes test-surface faces into evenly spaced points with outward-facing normals, using grid_step and a coplanarity tolerance; also computes the edge_taper weights. Used by preprocessing.
  2. Voxelization (voxelization.py): converts the max-volume mesh into a dense cubic boolean grid at the configured voxel_size. Used by preprocessing.
  3. Meshing (meshing.py): removes voxel clusters smaller than min_voxels and converts the carved voxel mask back into a triangle mesh, either as cubic voxel faces or via SDF smoothing + marching cubes + Taubin polishing. Used by exporting.

docs.text:
UrbanSolarCarver: test-surface sampling

Samples the test surfaces into the points and normals that rays start from, and the analysis-mesh quads that show one face per sample point. Used by preprocessing.

Pipeline entry point

Public API

discretize_surface_with_normals(mesh, sample_step=1.0, coplanarity_tol_deg=5.0, edge_taper=0.0) Split the mesh into connected components, sample each planar one, and return points, normals, an AnalysisMesh, weights, and taper statistics.

AnalysisMesh Quad mesh with one face per sample point; serialised to analysis_mesh.json.

Internal helpers

_mesh_boundary_loops(mesh), _sample_boundary_edges(polygon, ...) Boundary extraction and extra samples along boundary edges.

docs.title: plane_frame(surface_normal)
docs.text:
Return two orthonormal vectors spanning the plane orthogonal to surface_normal.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default surface_normal (3,) array_like

Plane normal (need not be unit length).

required

Returns:

Type Description axis_u, axis_v : (3,) np.ndarray

Unit vectors with cross(axis_u, axis_v) equal to the unit normal, so (axis_u, axis_v, normal) is a right-handed frame.

Raises:

docs.text:
Sample points on a regular grid over one planar submesh.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default mesh Trimesh

Single planar connected component (convex or not, with or without holes).

required sample_step float

Spacing of the sampling grid in world units.

1.0 include_boundary bool

If True, keep grid points that fall on the polygon boundary; otherwise drop them. Extra points seeded along the boundary edges (_sample_boundary_edges) are added in both cases.

True edge_taper float

Design-constraint taper distance (world units). When > 0, each sample gets a weight ramping linearly from 0 at the component outline (exterior and holes) to 1 at edge_taper from it.

0.0

Returns:

Name Type Description points (N, 3) float64 np.ndarray

Sample locations in world coordinates.

normals (N, 3) np.ndarray

Unit normal, the same for every point, oriented to agree with the area-weighted normal of the mesh faces.

quad_verts (4N, 3) float64 np.ndarray

Corner positions of one analysis-mesh quad per sample point.

docs.text:
Sample the nearly planar connected components of a mesh and return point/normal pairs.

Each connected component whose faces all lie within coplanarity_tol_deg of the component's area-weighted mean normal is sampled with sample_planar_surface; other components are skipped with a UserWarning. The quad analysis mesh has one face per sample point, suitable for per-face colouring (e.g. "LB Spatial Heatmap" in Grasshopper/Rhino).

Name Type Description Default mesh Trimesh

Input triangle mesh (test surface).

required sample_step float

Sampling grid spacing in world units.

1.0 coplanarity_tol_deg float

Maximum face-normal deviation (degrees) to consider a component planar.

5.0 edge_taper float

Design-constraint taper distance (meters): sample weights ramp from 0 at each component's outline to 1 at edge_taper inward. Distances are measured in the component's plane, which the coplanarity check guarantees exists.

0.0

Name Type Description points (N, 3) float32 np.ndarray

Sample points (centroids of the analysis-mesh quads).

normals (N, 3) float32 np.ndarray

Outward-facing normals at each sample point.

analysis_mesh AnalysisMesh or None

Combined quad analysis mesh, or None if no points were sampled.

weights (N,) float32 np.ndarray

Edge-taper design weights in [0, 1]; all ones when edge_taper == 0.

Per-component taper statistics (empty when edge_taper == 0). Components that never reach full weight (narrower than ~2× the taper) also emit a UserWarning, so the user knows that geometry is partly or wholly excluded from the protected program.

docs.title: voxelize_solid_warp(vertices, faces, grid_origin, voxel_size, resolution, device)
docs.text:
Solid-voxelize a triangle mesh by parity ray casting along x, y and z against a Warp BVH (bounding volume hierarchy).

A voxel is occupied when at least 2 of the 3 axis parity tests find its centre inside (a majority vote, so one axis confused by a small hole or a grazing ray does not decide the result; trimesh's orthographic fill uses the same idea), or when the mesh surface passes through it. Runs on CUDA or the Warp CPU device; voxelization.py uses trimesh's slower rasterize-and-fill only when this returns None, and lets anything it raises propagate.

Returns:

Type Description ndarray | None

(resolution, resolution, resolution) bool occupancy array, or None when the Warp backend is unavailable on device.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If the mesh has no vertices or no faces.

docs.title: urbansolarcarver.meshing
docs.text:
UrbanSolarCarver: meshing

Cleans the carved occupancy grid and turns it into the output mesh. Used by exporting.

Overview

Two meshing modes are supported:

1) Cubic (apply_smoothing == False) - Clean the binary grid: drop small connected components, then drop occupied voxels with fewer than 2 occupied neighbours in their 3×3×3 neighbourhood. - Triangulate with the shared-vertex cubic mesher (_cubic_mesh_from_occupancy).

2) Smoothed SDF (apply_smoothing == True) - Convert occupancy to a signed distance field (SDF) in voxel units. - Light Gaussian blur, then edge-preserving Perona–Malik diffusion; the result is kept only within 2 voxels of the zero level. - Pick an iso value that preserves the original inside volume. - Extract a surface with marching cubes (scikit-image). - Optionally run a short Taubin polish (0 to 6 iterations) after cleanup.

Pipeline entry point

finalize_mesh(carved_grid, grid_origin, settings, voxel_size) Clean the carved grid and mesh it with the cubic or smoothed path.

Public API

prune_voxels(voxels, min_voxels) Remove 26-connected components smaller than min_voxels.

prune_voxels_morph(voxels, min_voxels) Cleanup for the cubic path: component prune, then the neighbour-count filter described above. Only removes voxels; no erosion or closing.

mesh_from_voxels(voxels, min_corner, voxel_size) Build a blocky mesh from the binary grid. Returns an unprocessed Trimesh.

mesh_from_voxels_smoothed(voxels, min_corner, voxel_size) Build a smooth mesh by contouring a smoothed SDF with marching cubes. Uses a volume-matched iso to avoid systematic thinning.

cleanup_mesh(mesh, min_face_count=100, light=False) Fix winding/normals (unless light), weld vertices, drop small fragments.

polish_mesh_taubin(mesh, iters=2) Optional Taubin polish after the SDF + marching cubes path, at most 6 iterations.

Internal helpers

_cubic_mesh_from_occupancy(voxels, min_corner, voxel_size) Vertex and face arrays for the cubic mesher.

_voxel_presmooth(field_bool) SDF build + Gaussian + narrow-band Perona–Malik diffusion.

_pm_anisotropic_diffuse(sdf, iters, k, tau) Edge-preserving diffusion stepper used by _voxel_presmooth.

_volume_matched_threshold(sdf, target_inside_voxels) Iso selection that matches the original inside count.

_median_edge_length(m) Median of unique edge lengths; used to normalize the Taubin polish.

Data types and units
  • Voxel grids: torch.Tensor, shape (D, D, D), uint8/bool, 1 = inside.
  • Meshes: trimesh.Trimesh in world coordinates.
  • voxel_size is in world units and is passed to marching cubes as the grid spacing.
Notes
  • The cubic path gives a blocky "voxel look" that is stable between runs. It applies no erosion, so thin volumes are kept.
  • The smoothed path operates in SDF space, not on the triangle mesh. This removes terracing while keeping the overall form.
  • The Taubin step is short and optional. Heavy smoothing belongs in SDF space, not on the mesh.

docs.title: prune_voxels_morph(voxels, min_voxels)
docs.text:
Light cleanup for the cubic (unsmoothed) path.

Steps
  1. Remove connected components (26-connectivity) with fewer than min_voxels voxels.
  2. Remove occupied voxels whose 3×3×3 neighbourhood (including the voxel itself) holds fewer than 3 occupied voxels, i.e. voxels with 0 or 1 occupied neighbours. This drops isolated specks and one-voxel spurs.

Only removes voxels, never adds them: adding would undo carving.

required

docs.title: polish_mesh_taubin(mesh, iters=2)
docs.text:
Apply a short Taubin smoothing pass to remove small ripples.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default mesh Trimesh

Modified in place.

required iters int

Number of trimesh Taubin steps, capped at 6. trimesh alternates steps (even steps shrink, odd steps inflate), so even values give complete shrink/inflate pairs. If 0 or less, the mesh is returned unchanged.

2

Returns:

Name Type Description mesh Trimesh

The same object, smoothed, with degenerate faces removed.

Notes
  • Uses fixed parameters λ = 0.28 and ν = 0.31 (trimesh's sign convention; μ = −0.31 in Taubin's notation).
  • Vertices are centred and scaled to unit median edge length during smoothing, then restored.
  • Intended only after the SDF + marching cubes path. Keep the iteration count small to avoid shape drift.

docs.title: I/O
docs.text:
Mesh loading and saving through Trimesh.

  • load_mesh reads a mesh file (PLY, OBJ, STL and the other formats Trimesh supports).
  • save_mesh writes a mesh; for PLY it switches to double-precision vertices when float32 would round the coordinates (georeferenced models far from the origin).
  • validate_inputs checks that the files a preprocessing run needs exist (meshes, and the EPW for the modes that read one).
  • load_meshes loads the maximum volume and the test surfaces, and reports coordinates that a float32 PLY file has rounded.

docs.title: urbansolarcarver.io
docs.text:
Mesh file input and output, and the preprocessing inputs.

load_mesh reads a mesh file (PLY, OBJ, STL...) into a trimesh mesh; save_mesh writes one, switching PLY to double-precision vertices when float32 would round georeferenced coordinates. validate_inputs checks that the files a preprocessing run needs exist, and load_meshes loads the maximum volume and the test surfaces, reporting coordinates that a float32 file has rounded.

docs.title: load_mesh(path)
docs.text:
Load a triangle mesh from file.

trimesh's default processing on load removes NaN/inf vertices and merges duplicate vertices; it does not fix winding or remove degenerate faces. fix_normals is then called: it makes the face winding consistent across connected faces, and for watertight meshes it also turns each closed body that is stored inside out so its normals point outward.

Raises:

Type Description InputError

If path is not a file, if trimesh cannot parse it, or if it has no triangles (empty, or only points or curves). Without the last check the problem would only show up later as an empty voxel grid.

docs.title: float32_resolution(coords)
docs.text: Spacing between adjacent float32 values at the largest |coordinate|.

docs.title: save_mesh(mesh, path)
docs.text:
Save a mesh to disk, creating the output directory if needed, and return the absolute file path.

The format follows the file extension. PLY is written with float64 vertices when float32 spacing at the largest coordinate exceeds 1 mm (as with georeferenced coordinates), and GLB with its offset in the node (save_glb); otherwise trimesh's exporter is used. STL can only hold float32 vertices, so a float32_coordinates issue is reported when that rounds them by more than 1 mm.

docs.title: Pipeline
docs.text:
USC runs in three stages: preprocessing, thresholding, exporting, with massing as an optional fourth that reads the thresholding output like exporting. Each stage writes a manifest, last, after all its other outputs; the next stage reads it, so you can re-run thresholding with different parameters without recomputing scores. Every manifest has a random run_id, new on every run of its stage, and every manifest after preprocessing records the run_id of the manifest it was built from (upstream_run_id); a stage refuses an upstream that was re-run since (StageChainError). Manifests store paths relative to their own folder, so a run folder can be moved or copied. A stage first deletes the manifest and the outputs of its previous run in its folder, so a failed run leaves no manifest.

run_pipeline() runs the stages needed for what you ask it to produce, in one call. For finer control, call each stage individually.

from urbansolarcarver import load_config, run_pipeline

# One-shot: preprocessing, thresholding, exporting
result = run_pipeline(load_config("config.yaml"), out_dir="outputs")
print(result.exporting.export_path)

# Decomposed
from urbansolarcarver import preprocessing, thresholding, exporting
from pathlib import Path

cfg = load_config("config.yaml")
pre  = preprocessing(cfg, Path("outputs/preprocessing"))
thr  = thresholding(pre, cfg, Path("outputs/thresholding"))
exp  = exporting(thr, cfg, Path("outputs/exporting"))

docs.title: run_pipeline
docs.text:
run_pipeline(config, out_dir, produce=("exporting",), start_from="preprocessing", context=None) runs start_from and every later stage on the path to the stages in produce. Each stage writes into <out_dir>/<stage>; a stage before start_from is not run, and the next stage reads its output from its folder in out_dir.

# Floor plates as well as the mesh: preprocessing and thresholding run once
result = run_pipeline(cfg, "outputs", produce=["exporting", "massing"])
print(result.exporting.export_path, result.massing.plates_path)

# Change a threshold setting and reuse the scores already in outputs/preprocessing
cfg = load_config("config.yaml", ["carve_fraction=0.5"])
result = run_pipeline(cfg, "outputs", start_from="thresholding")
assert result.preprocessing is None   # it did not run in this call

The PipelineResult has one attribute per stage (preprocessing, thresholding, exporting, massing): the Result of a stage that ran in this call, None for the others. Its issues are the conditions noticed during the call (see Issues and run context). A start_from stage that is not on the path to a produced stage raises ValueError; a missing or stale upstream output raises StageChainError.

docs.text:
The stages to run, in pipeline order, to bring produce up to date.

Compares settings only; whether an input file changed, or whether a stage was ever run, is for the caller to decide.

  • Preprocessing effective values differ: preprocessing, thresholding and the produced leaves (exporting, massing).
  • Else thresholding differs: thresholding and the produced leaves.
  • Else each produced leaf whose own effective values differ.

Only stages that produce needs are listed, so producing "preprocessing" alone stops the list there. With no previous_config, every stage needed for produce is listed. Raises ValueError for a name that is not in :data:PIPELINE_STAGES.

docs.title: Issues and run context
docs.text:
Conditions that are not errors (settings the mode ignores, nothing carved, a footprint that could not be read, ...) are reported as issues: an Issue has the stage it was noticed in, a short code and a message. Each stage Result has issues, and PipelineResult.issues holds those of the whole call. Without a run context the engine also emits each issue as a warning.

A RunContext passed to run_pipeline collects the issues, calls on_progress(stage, done, total) as a stage advances, and stops the run when cancel() is called (RunCancelled; stages that finished keep their output). report_issue(code, message) records an issue on the active context.

from urbansolarcarver.run_context import RunContext

context = RunContext(on_progress=lambda stage, done, total: print(stage, done, total))
result = run_pipeline(cfg, "outputs", context=context)
for issue in result.issues:
    print(issue.stage, issue.code, issue.message)

docs.title: Preprocessing
docs.text: Voxelizes the max volume, samples the test surfaces, generates rays toward sky patches (or sun positions, or the tilted-plane direction), traces them through the voxel grid, and writes per-voxel obstruction scores to scores.npy.
